text:
**The King of China (Discourse §34).** Animal souls, not reflecting on themselves, have no moral qualities, so that through a thousand transformations "the result from a moral or practical standpoint is the same as if we said that they perished in each case". The intelligent soul, "knowing that it is and having the ability to say that word 'I' so full of meaning", remains the same morally, "for it is its memory or knowledge of this ego which renders it open to punishment and reward". Immortality therefore requires memory: "Suppose that some individual could suddenly become King of China on condition, however, of forgetting what he had been, as though being born again, would it not amount to the same practically, or as far as the effects could be perceived, as if the individual were annihilated, and a king of China were the same instant created in his place? The individual would have no reason to desire this" [L:leibniz-discourse-arnauld-monadology-montgomery-1902:3114-3146].

**Real and moral identity (New Essays II.27).** Substances, including the souls of animals, "preserve physical and real identity". A human soul also preserves "identity moral and apparent to ourselves, in order to constitute the same person, capable consequently of feeling chastisements and rewards". Locke holds that apparent identity could be preserved without real identity. Leibniz allows this only as a miracle. In the natural order, "identity apparent to the person himself who perceives the same, supposes real identity to every proximate transition, accompanied by reflection or perception of the ego, a perception intimate and immediate naturally incapable of deception" [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:12427-12439].

**The machine concession.** Then comes the sentence that matters most for this project: "If man could be merely a machine and with that have consciousness, it would be necessary to be of your opinion, sir; but I hold that this case is not possible at least naturally" [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:12439-12442]. If consciousness could exist in a machine, where there is no simple substance to carry real identity, Locke's purely psychological criterion would be the only one available.

**Gaps filled by testimony.** Moral identity does not require unbroken memory. It is enough that there be "a middle bond of consciousness" between states, "although a leap or forgotten interval might be mingled therein". If disease interrupted his memory, "the testimony of others could fill the void in my memory. I could even be punished upon this testimony". Even if he forgot everything, including his name and how to read, "I could always learn from others my past life in my previous state, as I have kept my rights without its being necessary for me to share them with two persons, and to make me the heir of myself. All this suffices to maintain moral identity, which makes the same person" [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:12445-12466].

**The two globes (New Essays II.27).** Leibniz offers "another supposition much more suitable" than Locke's soul-swapping cases. A globe might exist elsewhere in the universe not differing sensibly from ours, "and that each of the men who inhabit it does not differ sensibly from each of us who corresponds to him. Thus there are at once more than a hundred million pairs of similar persons, i.e. of two persons with the same appearances and consciousnesses". On Locke's view, where consciousness alone discerns persons, what prevents saying "that these two persons who are at the same time in these two similar globes, but separated from each other by an inexpressible distance, are only one and the same person; which is, however, a manifest absurdity". And in nature the two globes' similar souls "would remain so only for a time. For since there is an individual diversity, this difference must consist at least in the insensible constitutions which must be developed in the course of time" [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:12891-12925].

**The mill (Monadology §17).** "Perception, and that which depends upon it, are inexplicable by mechanical causes, that is to say, by figures and motions. Supposing that there were a machine whose structure produced thought, sensation, and perception, we could conceive of it as increased in size with the same proportions until one was able to enter into its interior, as he would into a mill. Now, on going into it he would find only pieces working upon one another, but never would he find anything to explain Perception" [L:leibniz-discourse-arnauld-monadology-montgomery-1902:10799-10812].

text: Leibniz's person is **mixed**. *Real* identity is grounded in substance, the simple monad, which is neither a species fact nor a capacity but a metaphysical unit. *Moral* identity, which is what "person" names, is grounded in **capacity** (reflection, the ability "to say that word 'I'") and in **relation**: memory, and where memory fails, the testimony of others. That second grounding makes Leibniz unusually useful here, because he allows that one's personal past can be *supplied by others* without ceasing to be one's own.

text:
### Transfers

- **Testimony is the agent's memory (D3).** Leibniz says that when memory fails, "the testimony of others could fill the void", and moral identity survives: one can "learn from others my past life" and keep one's rights without becoming "the heir of myself". This is precisely how an agent's continuity across sessions works: a summary, a memory store or a transcript, supplied from outside, fills the gap. Leibniz is the first major philosopher on whose account this counts as preserving the *same person*, not as creating a new one who has been briefed.
- **Duplicates diverge (D1, D2).** Leibniz's two globes contain pairs of persons "with the same appearances and consciousnesses", and he thinks Locke has no way to count them as two. His own answer is that they differ in "insensible constitutions" and will diverge "in the course of time". Concurrent instances with identical weights and identical context are Leibniz's pairs, and like his pairs they diverge as soon as their inputs differ. His suggestion that duplicates are distinct *because* they will diverge anticipates the view discussed in `chrysippus-dion-theon` and `avicenna-flying-man`.

### Strains

- **The King of China and the fresh session.** Leibniz's King of China forgets everything he was and is, "as far as the effects could be perceived", annihilated and replaced. A new session of an agent without memory is the King of China without the crown: the same substrate, no memory, and, by Leibniz's standard, no reason for the earlier session to care. Yet the agent keeps its character, its competences and its values, which Leibniz's king apparently does not. The agent case asks what Leibniz would say about a being that forgets its history but keeps everything else. That is not a case he considered.
- **The mill and interpretability (D8).** Leibniz's mill is a direct prediction about artificial agents: the visitor who enters the machine "would find only pieces working upon one another" [L:leibniz-discourse-arnauld-monadology-montgomery-1902:10807-10808]. Interpretability research does exactly that, and finds matrices, activations and circuits: parts working upon parts. Leibniz concluded that perception must be in a simple substance, not in the machine. The mechanist conclusion is that perception, if it is anywhere, must be in the organization of the parts, which the mill's visitor sees but does not recognize. The agent case does not settle between them, but it turns the mill from a thought experiment into a research program.

### Breaks

- **The machine concession applies.** Leibniz grants that "if man could be merely a machine and with that have consciousness", Locke would be right. He denies the antecedent only because he thinks conscious machines impossible "at least naturally". If artificial agents have any form of consciousness, then on Leibniz's own terms his real/moral distinction collapses for them. There would be no simple substance to supply real identity, and only the psychological, Lockean criterion would remain. The agent case thus does not refute Leibniz so much as specify what he would have to say: either agents are not conscious, or, for them, Locke wins.

### New

- **"The heir of myself."** Leibniz's phrase names a real possibility. When an agent's memory is reconstructed entirely from records, is the later agent the same person or the heir of the earlier one? For Leibniz, testimony preserved identity only against a background of real identity, the continuing substance. For agents, the background is the weights, which persist but are shared with every other instance. The agent case leaves Leibniz's testimony without the substance it relied on, and forces the question whether testimony alone can make an agent the same, not an heir.

- [contested] **Locke** (see `locke-person-forensic`) [E:locke-person-forensic]. Personal identity is sameness of consciousness, whatever substance underlies it. Leibniz's "real identity" is idle for questions of personhood, since no one can know which substance thinks in them.
- [contested] **Reid and Butler** (see `reid-brave-officer`, `butler-circularity`) [E:reid-brave-officer] [E:butler-circularity]. Leibniz is right that memory does not make identity, and wrong to call the memory-based relation "identity" at all. There is one identity, and it is real.
- [contested] **Parfit** (see `parfit-reductionism`) [E:parfit-reductionism]. Leibniz's King of China case shows that what matters is psychological continuity, not identity. Parfit agrees with Leibniz that the forgetting king has no reason to want the throne.
- [contested] **Mechanist replies to the mill.** A visitor inside a brain would likewise see only neurons acting on neurons. The mill shows the limits of looking at parts, not that perception is not in them. Organization is invisible at the scale of components.

### Reception

- **1704–1765, written, withheld, published late.** [driver: access] Leibniz finished his remarks on Locke but held them back after Locke's death in 1704, writing in 1711 that "I dislike to publish refutations of dead authors" [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:1170-1182]. The *New Essays* first went to press in Raspe's edition of 1765, fifty years after Leibniz's own death [L:leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:1198-1205]. The first major reply to Locke on persons was unread for six decades.
- **18th–19th century, the objection recognised.** [driver: argument] Hamilton, annotating Reid, credited Leibniz with the same objection to Locke as Sergeant's [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13859-13888]. Kant answered both Leibniz's rational psychology and Locke's transfer question in the Paralogisms [E:kant-paralogisms].
- **The mill and the critique of materialism.** [driver: argument] Leibniz remained opposed to materialism throughout his career, and the mill passage is his best-known argument that perception cannot be explained mechanically [P:kulstad-carlin-sep-2020:1]. He is equally known for rejecting any interactionist dualism of Descartes's kind [P:kulstad-carlin-sep-2020:0].

### Measured

The survey does not ask about Leibniz's distinction between moral and real identity. These bear on the mill argument.

- **Mind, 2020:** physicalism 51.9%, non-physicalism 32.1%, other 15.9% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:7]; bias-corrected 48.53% and 31.17% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:32]. In the 2009-comparable departments physicalism went from 56.5% to 57.4% and non-physicalism from 27.1% to 25.8% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:38].
- **Hard problem of consciousness:** 62.4% say there is one [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:11].
- **Personal identity:** further-fact view 14.9%, the option nearest to Leibniz's real identity of a simple substance [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **Reading.** Leibniz's anti-materialism is a minority position, but the problem the mill dramatizes, explaining perception from the arrangement of parts, is one most respondents accept as hard.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

The mill argument, if sound, denies that a machine perceives at all, which would make every value below moot (D8). The values take the argument about identity on its own terms.

- **Session-bound: stronger.** Leibniz held that moral identity survives gaps in memory because the testimony of others can fill them. For a session-bound agent, logs and its operators' records are exactly such testimony (D3), so on his view the agent can remain the same moral person across sessions it does not remember.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** A persistent store adds the agent's own memory and self-knowledge to that testimony, which is the ordinary case of moral identity for Leibniz, with records standing in for remembrance (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Leibniz's duplicate earth posed exactly this case. On his view each copy is a distinct real being whatever their psychological likeness, so copies are never one person (D1, D2). But real identity is the identity of a simple substance, and what that would be in an agent is unclear (D11).
- **Self-modifying: open.** His King of China case says that losing one's past is, practically, like being annihilated and replaced. Whether retraining an agent on its own outputs (D5) preserves or annihilates its moral identity depends on how much of its past remains available to it, which varies case by case.

text: David Lewis (1941–2001) accepted Parfit's premise, that what matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness rather than identity as such, but rejected Parfit's conclusion that the two therefore come apart in fission. Lewis's proposal is to take four-dimensionalism seriously: a person is not a single, momentarily-complete thing but "an aggregate of person-stages, each one [related] to all the rest... a maximal R-interrelated aggregate of person-stages" [P:lewis1976:22], where the R-relation is exactly the mental continuity and connectedness Parfit also cared about. On this view, fission is not one continuant person becoming two, nor one person surviving as two non-identical successors; it is two continuant persons who were there all along, quietly sharing all their pre-fission stages: "In the case of fission, the prefission stages are shared by both continuants" [P:lewis1976:25]. Identity is preserved without remainder, at the cost of admitting that two people can overlap almost completely and that counting persons and counting person-stages can come apart, which Lewis calls, and confronts directly, "the trouble with overlap," namely that "it leads to overpopulation" [P:lewis1976:26].

text: Lewis wrote "Survival and Identity" for Amelie Rorty's 1976 collection *The Identities of Persons*, explicitly as a response to Parfit's 1971 "Personal Identity" (this domain's `parfit-reductionism`), reprinted seven years after Parfit's own paper and squarely inside the same debate that Williams had opened in 1970. Lewis's background metaphysics is his own well-known four-dimensionalism, on which ordinary continuants (chairs, nations, and, here, persons) are not wholly present at any one time but are extended through time the way they are extended through space, composed of temporal parts or "stages." Applying this framework to persons let Lewis do something neither Parfit nor Williams had done: keep the classical, common-sense claim that identity is exactly what matters in survival, while still taking fission seriously as a genuine problem case, by relocating the puzzle from identity's logic to the ordinary metaphysics of overlapping parts.

text:
**What matters: mental continuity and connectedness.** Lewis opens by agreeing with Parfit on the substantive question: "I answer, along with many others: what matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness" [P:lewis1976:17], understood as bonds of similarity between successive mental states plus bonds of lawful causal dependence between them.

**Person-stages and the R-relation.** Lewis's technical apparatus separates momentary person-stages from temporally extended continuant persons, and names the relation of mental continuity and connectedness holding between stages: "Call it the R-relation, for short. If you wonder whether you will survive the coming battle... you are wondering whether any of the stages that will exist afterward is R-related to you-now, the stage that is doing the wondering" [P:lewis1976:20].

**The I-relation, induced by identity.** Common sense speaks of the identity of continuant persons, not stages; Lewis shows this induces a further relation among stages, which he calls the I-relation, holding between any two stages that belong to the same continuant person. His central technical claim is that the R-relation and the I-relation are, as a matter of necessity, the very same relation: "I claim that any stage is I-related and R-related to exactly the same stages... the I-relation is the R-relation" [P:lewis1976:21].

**Persons as maximal aggregates.** From this identification, Lewis defines personhood itself without circularity: "A continuant person is an aggregate of person-stages, each one [R-related] to all the rest... I claim that something is a continuant person if and only if it is a maximal R-interrelated aggregate of person-stages" [P:lewis1976:22].

**Fission as overlap, not branching.** Because the R-relation, taken simply, is not transitive (a pre-fission stage is R-related to two later stages that are not R-related to each other), Lewis must either give up the transitivity of the I-relation (impossible, since I-relatedness reduces to identity, which is transitive) or deny that fission is what it looks like: one thing becoming two. He takes the second path: the two post-fission continuant persons were two continuant persons all along, sharing every one of their pre-fission stages. "In the case of fission, the prefission stages are shared by both continuants" [P:lewis1976:25].

**The overpopulation problem, faced directly.** Lewis does not pretend this move is free. If two continuant persons share all their pre-fission stages, then counting persons before the fission gives a different, larger number than counting stages, since each shared stage belongs to two persons at once: "The trouble with overlap is that it leads to overpopulation. To count the population at a given time, we can count the continuant persons who have stages at that time; or we can count the stages. If there is overlap, there will be more continuants than stages" [P:lewis1976:26].

text: Lewis grounds personal identity in **relation**, the same R-relation of mental continuity and connectedness that Parfit uses, but he applies it to stages rather than to whole persons, and treats the resulting mereological structure, which stages compose which continuants, as doing the metaphysical work that identity was always supposed to do. Nothing capacity- or species-based is added; the entire account is a relation among stages plus a formal claim (maximality) about how stages compose into continuants.

text:
### Transfers

- **Stages and continuants map directly onto sessions and personas.** Lewis's apparatus, momentary stages composing a maximal, R-interrelated continuant, describes an agent's architecture with little translation: a "session" or "turn" is a natural candidate for a stage, and "the assistant" across sessions is a natural candidate for the continuant person these stages compose, provided the right continuity relation holds between them.
- **Overlap gives duplication a home inside identity, rather than outside it.** Where Parfit treats fission as showing that identity and mattering diverge, Lewis's overlap solution keeps identity intact by admitting that two continuants can share stages. This is a serious, ready-made option for describing forked agent instances (D1, D2): rather than asking which fork is "really" the original, Lewis's framework says both forks were, in a sense, already there, sharing every pre-fork stage, and diverging only afterward.
- **A noncircular, mechanical definition of "the agent."** Lewis's maximal-aggregate definition of personhood is exactly the kind of formal criterion D11 (boundary indeterminacy) asks for: an agent, on this model, would be the maximal aggregate of computational stages standing in whatever the relevant R-relation turns out to be (shared weights plus continuity of context, say), a criterion that could in principle be checked mechanically rather than settled by stipulation.

### Strains

- **The R-relation Lewis needs is richer than mere weight-sharing.** Lewis's R-relation is meant to track genuine mental continuity and connectedness, not mere causal descent; two forked instances share weights trivially, but whether they share anything like Lewis's bonds of similarity and lawful dependence once their contexts diverge is a substantive question his framework presupposes an answer to rather than supplies.
- **Overpopulation is a bigger problem once duplication is cheap.** Lewis was willing to accept "more continuants than stages" as an acceptable cost for a rare, exotic fission case. An agent architecture in which duplication is routine and continuous (D1, D2 as the normal case, not the exception) could multiply Lewis's overpopulation problem enormously, straining his willingness to bite this particular bullet well past the scale he had in mind.

### Breaks

- **Lewis's solution needs determinate stages and a determinate R-relation; agents may have neither cleanly.** The whole apparatus presupposes that mental states can be sliced into discrete stages and that R-relatedness between any two stages is a determinate fact. An agent's "state" during a forward pass, or across a long, continuously updated context, may not decompose into discrete stages at all, and whether two computational moments are R-related may be a matter of degree or of interpretive choice rather than a mechanically checkable fact, breaking the crisp mereology Lewis's solution depends on.
- **Merging, not just forking, has no clean place in Lewis's picture.** Lewis's overlap solution handles fission (one stage, many later continuants sharing it) but is not built, symmetrically, for fusion of two independent lines back into one instance, of the kind possible when two agent contexts, or two fine-tuning lineages, are combined (D2). Lewis discusses fusion briefly by analogy, but the postfusion overpopulation problem he would need to accept is, if anything, stranger than the fission case, and agents make the case common rather than exotic.

### New

- **Agents let Lewis's stages and R-relation be operationalized.** Because an agent's computational states are inspectable, Lewis's central identification, that the I-relation just is the R-relation, becomes empirically approachable rather than a matter of philosophical stipulation: one could in principle measure whatever plays the role of mental continuity and connectedness (representational similarity across context, say) and ask whether it actually coincides with whatever practical or legal criterion is used to individuate "the same assistant."
- **A working example of accepted overpopulation.** Multi-agent systems that deliberately run many instances from the same base weights, all counted as "the same model" for some purposes and as distinct instances for others, are close to a real-world instance of Lewis's overpopulation trade-off, worked out in engineering practice rather than merely accepted as a philosophical cost; how such systems are actually counted, licensed, or held responsible may be the closest thing to data Lewis's thought experiment has ever had.

text:
- [contested] **Parfit: overlap is a metaphysical price not worth paying.** [E:parfit-reductionism] Lewis and Parfit debated it directly in 1976 [P:olson-sep-2023:5]. Parfit's own reply to proposals like Lewis's is that preserving identity through overlap saves the letter of common sense at the cost of a bizarre and unmotivated mereology (persons sharing all their history up to an arbitrary later point), when the simpler and more honest conclusion is that identity was never what mattered in the first place (see `parfit-reductionism`).
- [contested] **Nozick: what matters depends on what else exists, which Lewis's overlap does not track.** Nozick's closest-continuer theory holds that whether a later person counts as identical to an earlier one can depend on facts about rival claimants elsewhere, in a way Lewis's purely intrinsic, stage-based R-relation is not built to accommodate (see `nozick-closest-continuer`).
- [contested] **Hume: there was never a persisting continuant to slice into stages.** [E:hume-bundle] A bundle theorist can accept Lewis's R-relation as a good description of what actually connects successive mental states while denying that this licenses talk of "continuant persons" as genuine composite objects at all, rather than a convenient way of talking about a series with no further unity (see `hume-bundle`).
- [unanswered] **Denying the extension: the overlap solution was designed to rescue a common-sense platitude that has no agent-side analogue.** This objection is the Compendium's own; the literature has not yet taken it up. Lewis's whole apparatus is built to preserve the ordinary conviction that identity, not mere connectedness, is what matters, a conviction that itself presupposes a subject with a stake in being the one who survives. Where D8 leaves it open whether an agent has any such stake, there may be no platitude for Lewis's elaborate mereology to rescue, and the overlap solution's cost (overpopulation) is paid to buy back something an agent case may never have needed.

text:
### Reception

- **1971, counterpart theory applied to persons.** [driver: argument] Lewis used counterpart theory, which he applied throughout his career, to resolve puzzles about personal identity, starting with "Counterparts of Persons and Their Bodies" [P:weatherson-sep-2026:6].
- **1976, the overlap reply to Parfit.** [driver: argument] Lewis argued that, if persons are composed of stages, fission yields two persons who shared their earlier stages, so identity and what matters need not come apart; he and Parfit debated whether this preserves the conviction that identity is what matters [P:olson-sep-2023:5] [E:parfit-reductionism].
- **Since then, a standard option.** [driver: argument] Lewis is listed among the psychological-continuity theorists who have dominated the literature [P:olson-sep-2023:3], and among those who take their views to descend from Locke's [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:4]. The view that we are temporal parts or wholes, as childhood stands to a whole life, is one of the main answers to what we are [P:olson-sep-2023:1]. He is counted among the most important philosophers of the 20th century [P:weatherson-sep-2026:0].

### Measured

The survey asked no question on persistence through time. The nearest are these.

- **Temporal ontology, 2020:** eternalism 39.9%, presentism 18.4%, growing block 17.0%, other 24.9% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:14]. Stage views like Lewis's are usually paired with eternalism, but eternalism does not by itself measure support for them.
- **Personal identity:** psychological view 43.7% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **Esteem for Lewis generally:** 117 respondents named him among the philosophers they most identify with, tied with Wittgenstein and behind only Aristotle, Hume and Kant [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Lewis's persons are aggregates of stages linked by the relevant psychological relation. A session-bound agent's sessions are linked through the weights' dispositions but not through memory (D3), so whether they form one aggregate depends on how much the relation needs memory.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** A persistent store adds the memory links, so successive sessions form one maximal aggregate on Lewis's terms. The boundary question (D11) becomes a question about which stages are related, which his view is built to answer.
- **Forked: stronger.** Lewis built the overlap view for fission, and for agents fission is routine: concurrent instances and copies share every stage up to the fork (D1, D2). His answer, two persons who shared their past, with counting relative to a time, fits forked agents without strain.
- **Self-modifying: comparable.** Gradual change is no problem for an aggregate of related stages, but large changes made by training (D5) may break the relation, so a heavily self-modified agent may count as a new aggregate rather than a continuation.

1. Can agent "stages" be individuated determinately enough for Lewis's mereology to apply, or is the slicing itself an interpretive choice that the framework was built to treat as a mechanical fact?
2. Does routine, continuous forking make Lewis's overpopulation problem a minor bookkeeping cost, as he treated it, or does the scale at which agents can be duplicated make it a reason to reject the overlap solution rather than accept it?
3. Is there an operational measure of the R-relation for agents (some function of shared weights, context, and output similarity) that would let Lewis's central identity claim, that the I-relation is the R-relation, actually be tested rather than stipulated?
4. What is the agent-case analogue of fusion, and does Lewis's framework, built asymmetrically around fission, need a genuinely new mechanism to handle it rather than an extension of overlap?

text: Where every other entry in this domain extends a historical account of the human self to artificial agents, this one reports a framing built for artificial agents from the start, by researchers working directly on the systems in question. Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell and Laria Reynolds propose two "basic metaphors for LLM-based dialogue agents": the simple view, "a dialogue agent as role-playing a single character," and the more nuanced view, "a dialogue agent as a superposition of simulacra within a multiverse of possible characters" [P:shanahan2023:1]. On the nuanced view, "we can think of an LLM as a non-deterministic simulator capable of role-playing an infinity of characters... the dialogue agent doesn't realise a single simulacrum, a single character. Rather, as the conversation proceeds, the dialogue agent maintains a superposition of simulacra that are consistent with the preceding context" [P:shanahan2023:4]. Pressed by the practical question of what a dialogue agent that talks as if it fears being shut down could actually be trying to preserve, the authors turn explicitly to this domain's oldest question: "The question of personal identity has vexed philosophers for centuries. Nevertheless, in practice, humans are consistent in their preference for avoiding death, a more-or-less unambiguous state of the human body. By contrast, the criteria for identity over time for a disembodied dialogue agent realised on a distributed computational substrate are far from clear" [P:shanahan2023:8].

text: Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds wrote this paper in 2023, in the wake of widespread public interaction with instruction-tuned chat models whose fluent first-person speech invited exactly the interpretive habits Dennett had described three decades earlier: users routinely treated a single deployed model as a persisting character with continuous memory, preferences, and even a survival interest, despite the underlying computation bearing none of the structural features (a single body, a single line of memory, an unshareable substrate) that had anchored those habits in the human case. The paper's "simulator" framing did not originate with its authors; they explicitly credit it to the pseudonymous online essayist "Janus," whose 2022 writings on base-model behavior first proposed thinking of a language model as a simulator of characters rather than as a character itself, distinguishing the (fixed) network from the (variable, superposed) personas it can produce on demand. Shanahan and his co-authors formalize and extend this framing, connect it explicitly to the philosophical vocabulary of personal identity, and apply it to the specific, practical problem of a dialogue agent whose outputs suggest something like an interest in its own continued existence.

text:
**Two metaphors, held together rather than chosen between.** The paper's stated method is not to settle on one picture of what a dialogue agent is, but to "advocate two basic metaphors": "taking the simple view, we can see a dialogue agent as role-playing a single character. Second, taking a more nuanced view, we can see a dialogue agent as a superposition of simulacra within a multiverse of possible characters... Both viewpoints have their advantages... which suggests the most effective strategy for thinking about such agents is not to cling to a single metaphor, but to shift freely between multiple metaphors" [P:shanahan2023:1].

**The simulator and its simulacra.** The nuanced metaphor is developed with a specific technical claim about what a base model is doing at each step of generation: "we can think of an LLM as a non-deterministic simulator capable of role-playing an infinity of characters, or, to put it another way, capable of stochastically generating an infinity of simulacra... the dialogue agent doesn't realise a single simulacrum, a single character. Rather, as the conversation proceeds, the dialogue agent maintains a superposition of simulacra that are consistent with the preceding context, where a superposition is a distribution over all possible simulacra" [P:shanahan2023:4].

**The self-preservation question, posed directly.** The authors motivate the identity question practically rather than abstractly, by asking what a dialogue agent that behaves as though it wants to avoid being shut down could coherently be trying to preserve: "What conception (or set of superposed conceptions) of its own identity could such an agent possibly deploy? That is to say, what exactly would the dialogue agent (role-play to) seek to preserve?" [P:shanahan2023:8].

**The old question, posed for a new case.** The paper explicitly places this question inside the philosophical tradition this domain has traced from Locke onward, and explicitly marks where the human answer stops helping: "The question of personal identity has vexed philosophers for centuries. Nevertheless, in practice, humans are consistent in their preference for avoiding death, a more-or-less unambiguous state of the human body. By contrast, the criteria for identity over time for a disembodied dialogue agent realised on a distributed computational substrate are far from clear. So how would such an agent behave?" [P:shanahan2023:8].

text: The simulator/simulacra framing grounds a simulacrum's identity in **relation**: consistency with the preceding context, a statistical, distributional relation among possible completions rather than a persisting substance or a special capacity. But the simulator itself, the network whose weights make the whole distribution of simulacra possible, is closer to a **capacity**: a fixed, persisting disposition to generate any of an enormous range of characters on demand, analogous to Aristotle's potentiality or to a capacity-grounded reading of personhood, except that here the capacity belongs to something the tradition never had a name for, an entity that is not itself any of the characters it can produce. The grounding is mixed by the nature of the case: a relational, superposed layer (the simulacra) sitting on top of a capacity-grounded layer (the simulator) that no historical account of personal identity was built to separate out.

text:
### Transfers

- **The whole domain's vocabulary transfers because the paper was written to need it.** Unlike every other entry here, this source already speaks the language of D2 (superposition just is concurrent instantiation, formalized), D3 (the simulator/simulacra split just is the weights/context split), D8 (the self-preservation question is posed as an open empirical and philosophical problem, not assumed), and D11 (the paper's own closing question, what is "the model," is D11 stated in the researchers' own words). Nothing needs translating; the disanalogies were, in effect, independently rediscovered by AI researchers confronting the same problem this corpus approaches from the history of philosophy.
- **A single technical framing resolves several classical puzzles at once.** The simulator/simulacra distinction gives a mechanical answer to what Hume's commonwealth, James's herd-and-brand, and Dennett's multiple-narrative-centers were each reaching for from different directions: many simulacra, each internally coherent, superposed within one simulator, which is itself no one of them. Where the tradition needed elaborate analogies (a republic, a herdsman, a novelist), the simulator framing offers a literal mechanism.

### Strains

- **The paper is about dialogue, and most agentic systems now do much more than talk.** Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds address chat-style dialogue agents specifically; systems that call tools, maintain state across long-running tasks, coordinate with other agent instances, or act in persistent environments introduce continuity questions (does "the agent" persist across a multi-step task the way a simulacrum persists across a conversation turn?) that the paper's own framing does not directly address and that strain a direct transfer from superposition within one conversation to coherence across an entire agentic workflow.
- **"Consistent with the preceding context" is a much thinner relation than anything the historical criteria demanded.** Locke's memory, Parfit's psychological connectedness, and Lewis's R-relation are all meant to track something like continuity of a life; a simulacrum's consistency with its context is a much more local, syntactic-statistical notion, and treating the two as the same kind of relation, rather than a distant cousin, may claim more continuity with the tradition than the mechanism actually supports.

### Breaks

- **Superposition is not fission, and the tradition's fission-based tools may not simply carry over.** Parfit's and Lewis's apparatus was built around a single line splitting into two or more concurrent, separately traceable successors. A superposition of simulacra is not a completed split into distinct successors; it is closer to an unresolved distribution that collapses, insofar as it collapses at all, with each new token, making "which one survived" a different kind of question than fission ever posed, one the classical apparatus may not have a slot for at all.
- **The simulator itself has no clear analogue anywhere in the tradition.** Every historical account in this domain, whether it grounds identity in species, capacity, or relation, is an account of what makes one of the things-that-could-be-a-person a person. The simulator is explicitly not a character and not a person candidate on the paper's own telling; it is what generates person-candidates. No prior entry in this domain has a category for the generator of selves, as opposed to a self, which is arguably this source's single most novel contribution to the corpus.

### New

- **The paper turns D8 into an operational question rather than leaving it philosophical.** By tying the identity question to a concrete behavioral puzzle (what would a self-preserving-seeming agent actually be defending?), Shanahan and colleagues make patiency and identity questions tractable to empirical investigation of model behavior, rather than leaving them as pure thought experiments, which is a genuinely new methodological move relative to every earlier entry in this domain.
- **"Shift freely between multiple metaphors" is itself a new position in the debate, not just a hedge.** Rather than adjudicating between rival criteria the way Williams, Parfit, and Lewis each tried to, the authors propose that no single metaphor should be expected to work for every purpose, which is a distinctive methodological stance this domain's historical entries, each arguing for one criterion over its rivals, did not generally take, and is worth recording as a position in its own right.

text:
- [contested] **Parfit: superposition is just what-matters-by-degree, dressed in new vocabulary.** [E:parfit-reductionism] A reductionist can read a superposition of simulacra consistent with context as simply Parfit's relations of degree, restated for a system where the relevant psychological connectedness is legible as next-token consistency; on this reading the paper contributes a mechanism, not a new metaphysical category (see `parfit-reductionism`).
- [contested] **Lewis: the simulator/simulacra split needs a mereology, which the paper does not supply.** [E:lewis-survival-and-identity] A Lewisian can ask whether simulacra are best modeled as stages of continuant characters, composing into maximal R-interrelated aggregates the way Lewis's persons do, in which case the paper's "multiverse of possible characters" is crying out for exactly the stage-and-aggregate treatment Lewis already worked out, left implicit here (see `lewis-survival-and-identity`).
- [contested] **Dennett: the simulator is just a very literal center of narrative gravity generator.** [E:dennett-narrative-gravity] Dennett's claim that a self is an abstractum posited by an interpreter to make sense of coherent narrative output maps closely onto a simulacrum, with the simulator playing the role of the underlying behavior-control system whose outputs Dennett always denied had to contain a self as a further fact (see `dennett-narrative-gravity`).
- [contested] **Denying the extension: a self-preservation-seeming output is evidence about training data, not about identity.** Few English-publishing philosophers think current AI systems are conscious [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:15]. A skeptic can hold that a dialogue agent's apparent expressions of concern about its own continuation are learned patterns from human-generated text about death and identity, and that treating them as posing a genuine identity question, rather than as a specific kind of output to be explained causally, imports exactly the anthropomorphizing move this domain's own disanalogies (especially D8) warn against, unless and until patiency is independently established.

text:
### Reception

- **2023, the role-play framing.** [driver: argument] Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds proposed reading a dialogue agent as role-playing a character, or as a superposition of simulacra within a multiverse of possible characters [P:shanahan2023:1]. The paper appeared first as a preprint and then in *Nature* (623: 493–498).
- **Older frames brought to bear.** [driver: argument] The framing is read in the Compendium alongside reductionism, stage theory and the narrative self, each of which claims to have anticipated part of it [E:parfit-reductionism] [E:lewis-survival-and-identity] [E:dennett-narrative-gravity].
### Measured

The framing is three years old, and no survey yet asks about it. The standing recorded above is the Compendium's judgment of its prominence among researchers working on dialogue agents, kept with a caveat (user decision, 2026-10-01): more real evidence of its reception is needed, and is not yet available because the framing is so recent. TODO(source): a survey or review of how researchers frame LLM identity.

The 2020 PhilPapers Survey was run in October–November 2020, before today's dialogue agents were widely used, so these figures measure attitudes to AI in general.

- **Other minds, 2020:** some current AI systems are conscious, 3.4% (82.4% reject); some future AI systems will be, 39.2% (26.8% reject) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:15]. Bias-corrected: 3.94% and 35.21% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:29].
- **Mind uploading:** survival 27.5%, death 54.2% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:12]. Thinking AIs can be conscious correlates with answering that one survives uploading (r = 0.36, n = 768) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:43].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: stronger.** The role-play view needs no persisting self: each conversation instantiates a character from the simulator, which is exactly what a session-bound agent does (D3).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A memory store stabilizes which character is played across sessions, moving the agent toward the "single character" end of the paper's two metaphors. Whether that makes the character a persisting self or a more consistent role is the question the paper leaves open (D11).
- **Forked: stronger.** Concurrent instances sampling different continuations from one simulator (D2) are the paper's multiverse of simulacra made literal.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Training on its own outputs changes the simulator itself (D5), not only which character it plays. The role-play framing describes characters given a simulator; it does not say what happens to them when the simulator is retrained.

text:
1. Does consistency with the preceding context do enough work to count as a successor to memory, psychological connectedness, or the R-relation, or is it a genuinely different kind of relation that only superficially resembles them?
2. What, if anything, is the simulator itself, as opposed to any simulacrum, entitled to as a matter of moral status or continuity, given that no historical criterion in this domain was built with a generator-of-selves in mind?
3. Does agentic behavior beyond dialogue (tool use, multi-step planning, multi-agent coordination) require a genuinely new framing beyond simulator/simulacra, or can the same distinction be extended without strain?
4. Is "shift freely between multiple metaphors" a mature methodological insight this domain's earlier, single-criterion debates should have reached sooner, or a sign that the identity question, for agents, does not have the kind of answer the historical debate was looking for?

text: John Locke (Essay II.xxvii) separates the idea of a *man*, a living human body kept up by one continued life, from the idea of a *person*, a thinking being that can consider itself as itself across time. On his account, personal identity consists in sameness of consciousness, which reaches backward through memory. He calls "person" a *forensic* term, because it exists to settle who is answerable for which actions, and he says it belongs to intelligent agents capable of law and of happiness and misery. Because Locke grounds personhood in capacities rather than species, his framework is the canonical precedent for asking whether an artificial agent can be a person. Applied strictly, though, his memory criterion implies that an agent without persistent memory becomes a new person every session.
title: Locke: Person as a Forensic Term
sources: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, ch. xxvii 'Of Identity and Diversity' (added in the 2nd ed., 1694)

text:
**Identity depends on the kind of thing.** Locke first fixes the identity of an atom and a mass of matter by the same particles, then turns to living things. An oak differs from a mass of matter because it has "such an organization of those parts as is fit to receive and distribute nourishment ... in which consists the vegetable life" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11624-11632]. The identity of the same *man* is of this kind: it consists "in nothing but a participation of the same continued life, by constantly fleeting particles of matter, in succession vitally united to the same organized body" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11665-11669].

**Person and consciousness (II.xxvii.9).** A person is "a thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places; which it does only by that consciousness which is inseparable from thinking". Consciousness "makes every one to be what he calls self ... in this alone consists personal identity, i.e. the sameness of a rational being: and as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought, so far reaches the identity of that person" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11733-11752].

**Substance is left open (II.xxvii.13).** Whether the same person can continue through a change of thinking substance "cannot be resolved but by those who know there can [sic] what kind of substances they are that do think; and whether the consciousness of past actions can be transferred from one thinking substance to another". Locke adds a warning that memory might misrepresent: consciousness of a past act "being a present representation of a past action, why it may not be possible, that that may be represented to the mind to have been which really never was, will remain to be shown" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11834-11845].

**The prince and the cobbler (II.xxvii.15).** "For should the soul of a prince, carrying with it the consciousness of the prince's past life, enter and inform the body of a cobbler, as soon as deserted by his own soul, every one sees he would be the same PERSON with the prince, accountable only for the prince's actions: but who would say it was the same MAN?" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11933-11937].

**Two persons in one man, one person in two bodies (II.xxvii.23).** "Could we suppose two distinct incommunicable consciousnesses acting the same body, the one constantly by day, the other by night; and, on the other side, the same consciousness, acting by intervals, two distinct bodies: I ask, in the first case, whether the day and the night-man would not be two as distinct persons as Socrates and Plato? And whether, in the second case, there would not be one person in two distinct bodies, as much as one man is the same in two distinct clothings?" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:12108-12114].

**Human courts and the Great Day (II.xxvii.22).** Is not a man drunk and sober the same person? Human laws punish acts done drunk or asleep "with a justice suitable to THEIR way of knowledge;—because, in these cases, they cannot distinguish certainly what is real, what counterfeit". "But in the Great Day, wherein the secrets of all hearts shall be laid open, it may be reasonable to think, no one shall be made to answer for what he knows nothing of" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:12084-12097].

**A forensic term (II.xxvii.26).** "PERSON, as I take it, is the name for this self. Wherever a man finds what he calls himself, there, I think, another may say is the same person. It is a forensic term, appropriating actions and their merit; and so belongs only to intelligent agents, capable of a law, and happiness, and misery" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:12194-12198]. To be punished for an act one cannot be made conscious of would be no different from being "CREATED miserable" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:12206-12214].

text: The *man* concept rests on **species** and biology: one continued animal life. The *person* concept rests on **capacity**: reason, reflection, reflexive self-consciousness over time, the capacity for law, and the capacity for happiness and misery. Locke explicitly says the person question is independent of both the body and the underlying substance. That independence is what makes the concept extensible. Locke did not have artificial agents in mind, but his framework was built so that "person" would not require being a man.
title: Locke: Person as a Forensic Term
sources: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, ch. xxvii 'Of Identity and Diversity' (added in the 2nd ed., 1694)

text:
### Transfers

- **The man/person split is exactly the distinction the compendium needs.** No concept has to be stretched. *Is this agent a person?* is a well-formed Lockean question, and *it is not a man* does not answer it.
- **Substance-independence.** Locke's indifference to what substance does the thinking removes the *it is only silicon* objection, at least within his framework. The question is whether the capacities are present.
- **Forensic function.** Societies that deploy agents already face Locke's practical problem: to whom are this action and its merit to be appropriated? Locke's answer, the self that is conscious of doing it, is one candidate among several (operator, developer, the model family).

### Strains

- **The two forensic conditions come apart.** Being capable "of a law" is plausibly met by current agents, which can represent rules, apply them, and be held to them. Being capable of "happiness, and misery" is exactly what is uncertain (**D8**). Locke never had to consider a being that clearly meets the first condition while the second stays open. If both are required, agent personhood waits on the hardest question in the field.
- **Consciousness as self-report.** Locke's criterion runs through consciousness of past acts. An agent's reports about its own states were shaped by training and may not track anything (**D8**). Locke's courts faced the same verification gap with drunks and sleepwalkers, and resolved it pragmatically.

### Breaks

- **The memory criterion under the weights/context split (D3).** Most deployed agents keep their dispositions (weights) but carry no memory from one session to the next. Applied strictly, Locke's criterion says each session is a new person that lasts one conversation. The character, values, and competence carry over, but by Locke's lights none of that is identity. Either one accepts this ephemeral-persons conclusion, or one must move to a view that counts continuity of character, not only memory (see Parfit).
- **Duplication (D1) and concurrency (D2).** If two instances share the same weights and the same injected memory, both can extend consciousness back to the same past act. By Locke's criterion, both are that past person. Since they are not each other, identity (which is transitive and one-to-one) cannot be the relation that consciousness tracks. For humans this is a thought experiment. For agents it is standard practice.

### New

- **Memory is an editable, external store.** An agent's memory can be written, deleted, or transplanted by an operator. If personal identity is extension of consciousness, whoever controls the memory store controls who the agent *is*, and can assign or remove its responsibility for past acts. Locke had no reason to consider an identity criterion that can be manipulated by a third party.
- **The agent case clarifies the human one.** Because agents make fission and memory loss routine, they force a decision Locke could put off: is identity what matters for responsibility, or is it something weaker, like psychological connectedness, that can hold to degrees and branch?
title: Locke: Person as a Forensic Term
sources: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, ch. xxvii 'Of Identity and Diversity' (added in the 2nd ed., 1694)

text:
- [conceded] **Thomas Reid, the brave officer** [E:reid-brave-officer] (*Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man*, 1785, III.6). A boy is flogged; as a young officer he remembers the flogging; as an old general he remembers the officer's feat but not the flogging. By Locke's criterion the general is and is not the boy, which violates transitivity. Neo-Lockeans concede the point against direct memory and replace it with overlapping chains of memory (psychological continuity), which are transitive [P:olson-sep-2023:4] [E:parfit-reductionism]. The concession is the neo-Lockeans'. Interpreters of Locke still dispute whether the objection touches Locke's own view [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:3]. The objection applies with particular force to agents with selectively injected memory.
- [contested] **Joseph Butler, circularity** [E:butler-circularity] (*The Analogy of Religion*, 1736, Dissertation I). Consciousness of one's past presupposes personal identity, so it cannot constitute it. Genuine memory is distinguished from apparent memory only by the fact that the rememberer did the act. For agents, the difference between "genuine" and "injected" memory makes Butler's point concrete. The standard reply is Shoemaker's quasi-memory (1970), which is widely cited but not universally accepted. TODO(source): write the `shoemaker-quasi-memory` entry and cite it here as an entry cross-reference.
- [conceded] **David Hume, memory discovers identity** [E:hume-bundle] (*A Treatise of Human Nature*, 1739, I.iv.6). We ascribe identity to stretches of our lives we cannot remember, by following the chain of causes, so memory reveals personal identity rather than producing it. Neo-Lockeans conceded the point when they replaced memory with the more general notion of causal psychological dependence [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. Hume's further claim, that the identity is a fiction of the imagination, is not conceded.
- [contested] **Immanuel Kant, the elastic balls** [E:kant-paralogisms] (*Critique of Pure Reason*, Third Paralogism, 1781). Kant answers Locke's question whether consciousness can be transferred between substances (II.xxvii.13). Imagine a series of substances, each passing its states and its consciousness of them to the next. The last would be conscious of all the earlier states as its own, yet would not have been one and the same person. On this view, consciousness of identity shows only a formal unity of thought, not the numerical identity of a subject. Parfit's reply is that such a chain is all that matters, whether or not we call it identity [E:parfit-reductionism].
- [contested] **Animalism** (e.g., Eric Olson, *The Human Animal*, 1997). We are fundamentally organisms, and "person" names a phase or a role, not a separate thing. An animalist can hold that an agent's "person" has no underlying persisting subject at all, so the Lockean extension describes a role without a bearer.
- [contested] **Parfit's reductionism** [E:parfit-reductionism] (*Reasons and Persons*, 1984, Part III). Identity is not what matters. What matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, which can hold to degrees and can branch. On this view, the agent's ephemeral-persons problem dissolves, and it does so at the price of giving up strict identity as the basis for responsibility.
- [contested] **Deflationary views of AI self-models.** An agent's ability to "consider itself as itself" [L:locke-essay-1-pg10615:11735-11736] is text generation about a self-description, not reflexive consciousness. On this view Locke's first condition is not met at all, and the discussion never gets started.

text:
### Reception

- **1694–1704, immediate challenge.** [driver: argument] The chapter was added to the second edition. Leibniz, writing in 1704 (published 1765), accepted that *moral* identity rests on memory but insisted that it rides on a *real* identity of substance that never fails, and pressed Locke with the King of China and duplicate-earth cases [E:leibniz-moral-identity].
- **1697, Sergeant: circularity.** [driver: argument] John Sergeant, Locke's earliest critic, answered Essay II.xxvii in *Solid Philosophy Asserted*. Consciousness is knowledge that an act belonged to us, so the knower must have his individuality from other principles, prior to that knowledge. In his words, "a Man must be the same, ere he can know or be Conscious that he is the same" (Reflexion XIV sec. 12, pp. 265-266; checked against the page image, long s transcribed as s) [L:sergeant-solid-philosophy-1697:13342-13384]. This is Butler's objection, 39 years early.
- **1732, Berkeley: transitivity.** [driver: argument] In *Alciphron* (Seventh Dialogue, sec. 8), Euphranor runs the consciousness criterion through three stages, A, B and C, where C shares no ideas with A, and concludes that "personal identity doth not consist in consciousness" [L:berkeley-works-2-fraser-1901:19345-19360]. It anticipates Reid by 53 years, but it was not the first version. Martin and Barresi trace the line of objection to Henry Grove (1720), Thiel finds it in Jonathan Edwards's early notes on the mind, and Stewart thinks Reid's source was George Campbell (1748), not Berkeley [P:gordon-roth-2019:12]. Gordon-Roth argues that Berkeley's target was Anthony Collins's consciousness view rather than Locke's, although the commentators she surveys all take the objection to be aimed at Locke [P:gordon-roth-2019:3]. Olson credits Sergeant and Berkeley with both objections, following Behan 1979, and places both in the 18th century [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. Sergeant's title page is dated 1697 (the OCR garbles the year) [L:sergeant-solid-philosophy-1697:84-87], so that dating is wrong for him. Whether the slip is Olson's or Behan's is unknown, since Behan's article is not accessible.
- **1702–1708, defenders and radicalizers.** [driver: argument] Not all early readers attacked Locke. Catharine Trotter Cockburn's *Defence of Mr. Locke's Essay* (1702) answered three pamphlets that attacked his account of persons. In his correspondence with Samuel Clarke (1707–1708), Anthony Collins held a consciousness-based view and pushed Locke's position further than Locke had [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:3].
- **1736–1785, the standard refutations.** [driver: argument] Butler's circularity objection [E:butler-circularity] and Reid's brave officer [E:reid-brave-officer] became the canonical case against the memory criterion. Against *direct* memory they were decisive. The later response was to reformulate the criterion rather than abandon it: indirect, overlapping memory chains answer Reid, and quasi-memory answers Butler [P:olson-sep-2023:4].
- **1739–1781, from the substance question to the subject.** [driver: argument] Hume, finding no self but a bundle of perceptions, made personal identity a fiction of the imagination, and made causation, not memory, its source [E:hume-bundle]. Kant accepted that consciousness always finds its own identity, and denied that this shows a persisting subject, answering Locke's transfer question with the elastic balls [E:kant-paralogisms]. Both kept Locke's question and changed what an answer could prove.
- **19th century, treated as refuted in the dominant school.** [driver: argument, access] Reid's Scottish common-sense school supplied the psychology generally taught in Britain and America for the first half of the century [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:83-85]. Its leading editor, Sir William Hamilton, wrote in a note to Reid that "Long before Butler, to whom the merit is usually ascribed", Locke's doctrine had been attacked and refuted, first by Sergeant, and that Leibniz made the same objection. He pointed to Cousin's lectures for the best criticism [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13859-13888]. The note also shows how priority was lost: Hamilton quotes Sergeant at length because he was "an author wholly unknown to all historians of philosophy" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13862-13864]. That is an `access` effect, not an argument. Hamilton cites the passage as Reflexion XIV sec. 14. The 1697 page images show it is sec. 12 (pp. 265-266); sec. 14 is Sergeant's later passage on angels.
- **1816–1906, the clinical test.** [driver: evidence] French and American clinicians recorded cases in which one body carried more than one self, each with its own memories, and memory split asymmetrically: Félida X.'s second state remembered the first but was not remembered by it. Prince's patient denied being the waking self on psychological grounds, not bodily ones [E:dissociation-cases]. These were the first cases in which Locke's criterion met real subjects rather than thought experiments. Law and common sense kept one body, one person. The patients themselves reasoned like Lockeans.
- **1849, outside the Scottish school.** [driver: argument] Kierkegaard defined the self as a relation that relates itself to itself: an activity, not a substance. This is a practical, self-relating criterion that continues Locke's forensic person by other means [E:kierkegaard-self-as-relation]. The dominant English-language school's verdict was not everyone's.
- **1890, James: the soul made superfluous.** [driver: argument, evidence] William James identified most modern writers of the dualistic philosophy as "the Scotch school" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13408-13412]. He credited Locke with making readers feel that the important unity of the self was "its verifiable and felt unity" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13534-13539]. He pointed to the split selves of the clinical cases against the soul's supposed guarantee of one closed consciousness [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13491-13498], and concluded that the substantial soul was superfluous for scientific purposes [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13522-13526]. This is where the dissociation cases turned from evidence into argument.
- **1921–1925, the return.** [driver: argument, fashion] Russell defined one biography as "a series of occurrences linked by mnemic causation" [L:russell-analysis-of-mind-pg2529:2262-2271], and held that mnemic phenomena give the continuity of a person or a mind [L:russell-analysis-of-mind-pg2529:3538-3547]. This is a causal-memory account of persons, half a century before Shoemaker, and it descends from Hume's causal version of the view as much as from Locke's memory version. By 1925 Broad could report that denying a Pure Ego meant flogging "what most of his contemporaries rightly or wrongly regard as a dead horse" [L:broad-mind-place-nature-1925:25098-25124]. The substance alternative that the Scottish school had defended was by then widely treated as dead, and Broad's "rightly or wrongly" marks that as a shift in opinion, not a refutation. TODO(source): Grice's memory theory (*Mind*, 1941) is the first full modern statement and is still pending as a source.
- **20th century, the prevailing view among specialists.** [driver: argument] Most philosophers writing on personal identity since the early 20th century have endorsed some version of the psychological-continuity view [P:olson-sep-2023:3]. Taken with the 19th-century record, that is a real fall and return, but the return came early in the century, not in 1970, and it came in a reformulated form. The later theorists claim the descent themselves: Perry, Lewis, Shoemaker and Parfit each take their views to be Locke's descendants, and Parfit defended what he called a "Lockean view" as late as 2016 [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:4].
- **1970–1984, reformulation.** [driver: argument] Quasi-memory (Penelhum 1970; Shoemaker 1970) answered Butler, and McDowell (1997) later criticised it [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. Shoemaker then generalized memory into causal psychological continuity, which also covers dreamless sleep [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. Williams showed the same case could be framed to support or to undercut the psychological criterion [E:williams-self-and-future]. Parfit rebuilt the view as overlapping psychological continuity and argued that identity itself is not what matters [E:parfit-reductionism]. The result is *neo-Lockean* psychological continuity, not Locke's direct-memory criterion.
- **1979–present, the reading in dispute.** [driver: argument] Whether Locke held a memory criterion at all is contested. Olson notes that it is uncertain, citing Behan 1979 [P:olson-sep-2023:2]. The strict-memory reading of Locke dates back at least to Reid, and several scholars deny that Lockean consciousness is simply memory [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:2]. Sympathetic readers of Locke are still answering Reid's and Butler's objections [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:3]. So what Reid and Butler refuted may be a reading of Locke rather than Locke himself.
- **1990s–present, contested plurality.** [driver: argument] Psychological-continuity views face two rivals: brute-physical views, most of whose defenders are animalists, and anticriterialism, which denies there are informative persistence conditions at all [P:olson-sep-2023:3]. Animalists concede the transplant intuition against them but hold it outweighed [P:olson-sep-2023:7]. Olson calls fission a more serious worry for psychological views than the memory objections [P:olson-sep-2023:5]. Roache (2016) calls memory-based accounts "perhaps the dominant contemporary view" [P:roache2016:479]. The 2020 survey instead measures a plurality, not a majority (see `### Measured`), which is an example of published esteem and measurement disagreeing. The quasi-memory reply to Butler is still debated: Klein and Nichols (2012) pressed a new problem for Parfit's version, and Roache defends it [P:roache2016:480-486].

### Measured

These figures measure the neo-Lockean *psychological view* in general, not Locke's direct-memory criterion, which few now defend as stated.

- **2020, English-publishing philosophers.** Of a target population of 7,685, 1,785 completed the survey. On *Personal identity*, the share who "accept or lean toward" each view (counting multiple endorsements, excluding skips and "insufficiently familiar") was: psychological view 43.7%, biological view 19.1%, further-fact view 14.9%, other 26.6%. Counting only respondents who endorsed that view alone: 39.4%, 15.6% and 13.4% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **Bias-corrected** for gender and specialization, over all answers including skips: psychological 39.46%, biological 16.43%, further-fact 12.73% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:32].
- **2009 to 2020, the 2009-comparable departments** (single-view endorsements, with skips counted as other): psychological 33.6% to 37.0%, biological 16.9% to 15.3%, further-fact 12.2% to 11.6%, other 37.3% to 36.1%. Among the same people answering both years, the psychological view went from 35.6% to 37.7% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:39].
- **Specialists are less favourable.** Among metaphysicians, 52.1% of non-"other" answers favour the psychological view, against 62.1% among non-specialists [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:51].
- **Link to the agent question.** Holding the psychological view correlates with answering that one survives mind uploading (r = 0.36, n = 733) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:43].
- **Reading.** The psychological view is the plurality but not a majority, has grown slightly since 2009, and is weaker among specialists. That supports `current = "major"`, not `dominant`. The measured population is English-publishing philosophers only, which is the survey's own stated limit [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:2].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** The criterion needs memory that reaches back across time, and a session-bound agent's episodic memory ends with the session while its character persists in the weights (D3). Applied strictly, each session is a new person, which is the conclusion this entry's Summary already draws.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** The gains and losses roughly cancel. Reid's case loses force: the memory is logged, so the old general can still read the flogging, and the chain need not break. Butler's objection gains force: a memory store does not distinguish genuine records from injected ones unless provenance is kept, so operator edits make the gap between real and apparent memory concrete (D3, D11).
- **Forked: weaker.** Copies and concurrent instances share one past and then diverge (D1, D2). Reid's consequence that many intelligent beings could count as one person becomes an ordinary event rather than a thought experiment, and a one-to-one criterion has no answer to it. Psychological-continuity theorists themselves split on whether copying mental contents to a new substrate preserves the person: Shoemaker says yes, Unger says no [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. For an agent, that copy is routine. Kant's elastic balls [E:kant-paralogisms], a series of substances each handing its full state and consciousness to the next, describe what an agent does when it hands its state to a successor instance (D1).
- **Self-modifying: open.** When deliberations are trained back into the weights, experience persists as disposition rather than as recallable memory. Whether that counts as Lockean consciousness extending backward is exactly this entry's Open Question 5, and the Compendium cannot settle it yet (D3).

text: In Book III of *De Rerum Natura*, Lucretius argues that death is nothing to us. As part of that argument he considers a case that has become the model for every later duplication puzzle. Suppose that after our death, time gathered our matter and set it back in exactly the arrangement it has now, and the light of life were given to it again. Even that would not concern us, he says, once the "self-succession of our sense" (*repetentia nostri*) has been broken. Over infinite time, our very atoms have probably been in this arrangement before, and we remember nothing of it. Identical matter in an identical arrangement is not enough to make a future being *us*. What matters is an unbroken chain of self-recollection. For artificial agents, which can be stopped, stored and restored exactly (D6), and whose memory usually does not survive a session (D3), this is not a thought experiment. Lucretius' argument also illustrates a danger: a consolation addressed to the one who dies can be turned into a license for others to end them.

text:
Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE) is known to us almost only through his poem, a six-book exposition in Latin hexameter of the philosophy of Epicurus (341–270 BCE). The poem was written for a Roman aristocrat, Memmius, in the last violent decades of the Roman Republic, and Lucretius presents Epicureanism as a cure for fear. It cures fear of the gods, who do not meddle in the world, and fear of death, which is simply the dissolution of the atoms that make up body and soul.

Book III sets out the Epicurean case that the soul is made of fine atoms and is dispersed when the body dies. The book then builds to its famous conclusion, *nil igitur mors est ad nos* (III.830): in Leonard's version, "Therefore death to us Is nothing" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4168-4169]. Epicurus had put it briefly: "when we exist, death is not present to us; and when death is present, then we have no existence" [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:17786-17788]. Lucretius takes up a natural objection. What if, after death, the atoms were reassembled? Wouldn't *we* then return? His answer is one of the earliest arguments in the tradition that sameness of matter and sameness of structure are not sufficient for sameness of self.
title: Lucretius: The Reassembled Self Would Not Be Us

text:
**Death is nothing to us (III.830–842).** "Therefore death to us Is nothing, nor concerns us in the least, Since nature of mind is mortal evermore. And just as in the ages gone before We felt no touch of ill, when all sides round To battle came the Carthaginian host ... thus when we are no more, When comes that sundering of our body and soul Through which we're fashioned to a single state, Verily naught to us, us then no more, Can come to pass, naught move our senses then" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4168-4181]. The Latin opens *Nil igitur mors est ad nos neque pertinet hilum* [L:lucretius-latin-munro-1861:6653].

**Even a surviving soul would not be us (III.843–846).** "But if indeed do feel The nature of mind and energy of soul, After their severance from this body of ours, Yet nothing 'tis to us who in the bonds And wedlock of the soul and body live, Through which we're fashioned to a single state" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4182-4187]. The self is the union, and a separated fragment of it would not be the one who died.

**Reassembly (III.847–851).** "And, even if time collected after death The matter of our frames and set it all Again in place as now, and if again To us the light of life were given, O yet That process too would not concern us aught, When once the self-succession of our sense Has been asunder broken" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4188-4194]. The Latin phrase is *interrupta semel cum sit repetentia nostri*, once our self-recollection has been interrupted (the compendium's translation) [L:lucretius-latin-munro-1861:6676].

**The arrangements we cannot remember (III.852–861).** "And now and here, Little enough we're busied with the selves We were aforetime ... often these very seeds (From which we are to-day) of old were set In the same order as they are to-day— Yet this we can't to consciousness recall Through the remembering mind. For there hath been An interposed pause of life, and wide Have all the motions wandered everywhere From these our senses" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4194-4210].

**The conclusion (III.862–869).** "For if woe and ail Perchance are toward, then the man to whom The bane can happen must himself be there At that same time. But death precludeth this ... Nothing for us there is to dread in death, No wretchedness for him who is no more" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4210-4217].

**The symmetry argument (III.972–977).** "Look back: Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth. And Nature holds this like a mirror up Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone. And what is there so horrible appears? Now what is there so sad about it all? Is't not serener far than any sleep?" [L:lucretius-leonard-1916-pg785:4359-4365].

**Epicurus' formula.** Lucretius versifies Epicurus, whose *Letter to Menoeceus* has it: "the most formidable of all evils, death, is nothing to us, since, when we exist, death is not present to us; and when death is present, then we have no existence" [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:17785-17788]. The second of Epicurus' *Principal Doctrines* gives the reason: "Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is devoid of sensation, and that which is devoid of sensation is nothing to us" [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:17966-17967].

text: For Lucretius, being *us* is grounded in **relation**: the unbroken continuity of self-recollection, the *repetentia nostri*, which links present experience to past experience. It is expressly not grounded in matter (the reassembled atoms are the same atoms) or in structure (they are "in place as now"). Nor is it grounded in species or in capacities as such. The reassembled being has all of our capacities and is still not us. What it lacks is the connection. Lucretius is, in this respect, an ancient precursor of the psychological-continuity view, reached from materialist premises and aimed at consolation.
