text: Thomas Reid (1710–1796) gave Locke's memory criterion its most famous refutation. A boy is flogged for robbing an orchard. As a young officer he takes an enemy standard, remembering the flogging. As an old general he remembers taking the standard but has forgotten the flogging. By Locke's criterion the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, so by the transitivity of identity the general is the boy. But the general cannot remember the flogging, so by the same criterion he is not the boy. "Therefore the general is, and at the same time is not, the same person with him who was flogged at school." Reid drew two further consequences of Locke's view. If consciousness can be transferred, "two or twenty intelligent beings may be the same person". And if memory can be lost, "one intelligent being may be two or twenty different persons". His own view is that a person is "a monad" that "is not divisible into parts", that identity "supposes an uninterrupted continuance of existence", and that memory is evidence of identity, not what constitutes it. Personal identity, he says, "is the foundation of all rights and obligations, and of all accountableness". Each of Reid's consequences is an ordinary occurrence for artificial agents, and his closing claim sets out what is at stake.

text: Reid was a Presbyterian minister and then professor at Aberdeen and Glasgow, where he succeeded Adam Smith. He is the founder of the Scottish "common sense" school. He began as a follower of Berkeley and turned against the whole "way of ideas" after reading Hume, which he took to lead inevitably to skepticism about the external world, the self and causation. Reid's response was that certain beliefs, including belief in one's own continued existence, are "first principles" of human nature that philosophy must begin from, not prove. The *Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man* (1785) are the mature statement of this program. The chapters on identity sit within the essay on memory, because Reid thought memory and identity could only be understood together. He acknowledged Butler as his predecessor: Locke's account "has been censured by Bishop Butler ... with whose sentiments I perfectly agree" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13786-13788].

text:
**Identity requires uninterrupted existence.** "I see evidently that identity supposes an uninterrupted continuance of existence. That which has ceased to exist cannot be the same with that which afterwards begins to exist; for this would be to suppose a being to exist after it ceased to exist, and to have had existence before it was produced, which are manifest contradictions" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13541-13548]. So identity cannot strictly apply to pains or thoughts, which are successive: "The pain felt this day is not the same individual pain which I felt yesterday" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13548-13556].

**The person is indivisible.** All mankind, Reid says, place their personality "in something that cannot be divided, or consist of parts. A part of a person is a manifest absurdity." Amputation does not remove a part of the person: "The amputated member is no part of his person, otherwise it would have a right to a part of his estate, and be liable for a part of his engagements ... A person is something indivisible, and is what Leibnitz calls a monad" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13574-13588].

**The self is not its thoughts.** "My personal identity, therefore, implies the continued existence of that indivisible thing which I call myself. Whatever this self may be, it is something which thinks, and deliberates, and resolves, and acts, and suffers. I am not thought, I am not action, I am not feeling; I am something that thinks, and acts, and suffers" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13589-13596].

**Memory is evidence.** "The proper evidence I have of all this is remembrance ... my memory testifies, not only that this was done, but that it was done by me who now remember it" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13609-13614]. But memory does not make identity: "This remembrance makes me to know assuredly that I did it; but I might have done it, though I did not remember it ... To say that my remembering that I did such a thing ... makes me to have done it, appears to me as great an absurdity as it would be to say, that my belief that the world was created made it to be created" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13640-13652]. "I know who bare me, and suckled me, but I do not remember these events" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13636-13637].

**Perfect and loose identity.** "The identity of a person is a perfect identity: wherever it is real, it admits of no degrees; and it is impossible that a person should be in part the same, and in part different; because a person is a monad, and is not divisible into parts" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13661-13666]. The identity of bodies is different: of an old regiment, a tree, and a ship of war whose planks and timbers have all been replaced, "The identity, therefore, which we ascribe to bodies, whether natural or artificial, is not perfect identity; it is rather something which, for the conveniency of speech, we call identity ... and questions about the identity of a body are very often questions about words. But identity, when applied to persons, has no ambiguity, and admits not of degrees, or of more and less. It is the foundation of all rights and obligations, and of all accountableness; and the notion of it is fixed and precise" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13747-13768].

**Locke's strange consequences.** Locke's doctrine has consequences he was aware of: "(1.) Such as, that if the same consciousness can be transferred from one intelligent being to another, which he thinks we cannot show to be impossible, then two or twenty intelligent beings may be the same person. (2.) And if the intelligent being may lose the consciousness of the actions done by him, which surely is possible, then he is not the person that did those actions; so that one intelligent being may be two or twenty different persons, if he shall so often lose the consciousness of his former actions" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13838-13847].

**The brave officer.** "(3.) There is another consequence of this doctrine, which follows no less necessarily, though Mr. Locke probably did not see it. It is, that a man may be, and at the same time not be, the person that did a particular action. Suppose a brave officer to have been flogged when a boy at school for robbing an orchard, to have taken a standard from the enemy in his first campaign, and to have been made a general in advanced life; suppose, also, which must be admitted to be possible, that, when he took the standard, he was conscious of his having been flogged at school, and that, when made a general, he was conscious of his taking the standard, but had absolutely lost the consciousness of his flogging." It follows from Locke's doctrine that the general is the same person as the boy, by transitivity, and that he is not, since his consciousness does not reach the flogging. "Therefore the general is, and at the same time is not, the same person with him who was flogged at school" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13848-13912].

text: Reid grounds personhood in **capacity**, in the being that "thinks, and deliberates, and resolves, and acts, and suffers", and grounds personal identity in the uninterrupted existence of that indivisible being. Like Butler's, his is a "simple view": identity is a basic fact, known by memory and by the first principles of common sense, not analyzable into relations among states. Reid's grounding is explicitly not **relational**. Relations of similarity ground only the loose, verbal identity of bodies. Nor is it grounded in **species**. Reid speaks of "intelligent beings", and his account applies to any.

text:
### Transfers

- **"Two or twenty intelligent beings may be the same person" (D1, D2).** Reid offered this as a reductio of Locke. For agents it is simply how deployment works. Many instances receive the same memory store or context and are, by Locke's criterion, the same person. Reid's point transfers intact: if we reject that conclusion, Locke's criterion cannot be the criterion for agents either.
- **"One intelligent being may be two or twenty different persons" (D3).** The same weights, run in successive sessions with no memory between them, are Reid's single intelligent being that shall "so often lose the consciousness of his former actions" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13846-13847]. On Locke's criterion each session is a different person. Reid's reductio again describes ordinary operation.
- **The brave officer is an agent with a sliding context window.** An agent whose context holds only its most recent turns is in the general's position at every step. Turn 50 remembers turn 30, which remembered turn 10, but turn 50 does not remember turn 10. By Locke's criterion, the agent at turn 50 both is and is not the one that acted at turn 10. For agents, Reid's objection is not a thought experiment about old age. It follows from how context windows work.

### Strains

- **Uninterrupted existence (D6).** Reid's criterion is that "identity supposes an uninterrupted continuance of existence": what ceased to exist cannot be the same as what later begins. An agent paused and resumed has, on the most natural reading, ceased to exist as an activity and begun again. If the agent is the running process, Reid's criterion makes every resumption a new being. If the agent is the weights, which exist continuously on disk, the criterion is satisfied, but then the agent is the stored parameters, which do not think, deliberate or act. Reid's "something that thinks, and acts, and suffers" and his "uninterrupted continuance" pick out different candidates in an agent.

### Breaks

- **The indivisible monad has no agent counterpart (D11).** Reid holds that "a part of a person is a manifest absurdity", and that the person is "not divisible into parts". An artificial agent is divisible in every relevant sense. Its weights can be pruned, merged, split across machines or partially fine-tuned. Its context can be edited. Its tools can be removed. If personhood requires Reidian indivisibility, no artificial agent is a person, since there is no indivisible thing in it to be one. The alternative is to find in the agent something that behaves as a unit for the purposes Reid cared about, "rights and obligations, and ... accountableness", even though it is not metaphysically simple.

### New

- **Identity as the foundation of accountability, supplied by design.** Reid's closing thought is that personal identity "is the foundation of all rights and obligations, and of all accountableness". If agents lack Reidian identity (uninterrupted, indivisible, perfect), then whatever accountability agents bear must rest on something else: an institutional designation, a persistent record, an operator's liability. The agent case forces a question Reid could treat as closed. Can there be rights, obligations and accountability without the perfect identity he took to be their foundation? Or is the foundation itself something societies build?

text:
- [unanswered] **Locke's defenders; Shoemaker** (see `shoemaker-quasi-memory`). This reply is widely accepted, and few defend Reid's stronger conclusion against it [P:olson-sep-2023:4]. The brave officer refutes only a direct-memory criterion. Replace it with overlapping chains of memory (the general remembers the officer, who remembered the boy), and transitivity is restored. Reid's objection has shaped every modern psychological-continuity theory.
- [contested] **Parfit** (see `parfit-reductionism`) [E:parfit-reductionism]. Reid's consequences (1) and (2) show that psychological continuity can branch and fail, so it cannot be identity. That is correct, and it shows that identity is not what matters. Parfit accepts Reid's premises and rejects his conclusion.
- [contested] **Hume** (see `hume-bundle`) [E:hume-bundle]. The perfect, indivisible identity Reid appeals to is a fiction. His "invincible belief" in it is a fact about human psychology, not evidence of a monad.
- [contested] **Relational and institutional views.** Rights and accountability are grounded in social practice and law, which routinely assign them to entities without Reidian identity: corporations, regiments, states. Reid's own example of the old regiment shows that "loose" identity can bear historical responsibility.

text:
### Reception

- **1720–1748, the line before Reid.** [driver: argument] The transitivity objection predates Reid: Martin and Barresi trace it to Henry Grove (1720), Thiel finds it in Jonathan Edwards's notes, Berkeley made it in 1732, and Stewart argues that Reid's own source was George Campbell (1748) rather than Berkeley [P:gordon-roth-2019:12].
- **1785, the canonical version.** [driver: argument] The brave officer became the most popular and best-known form of the objection that Locke's view contradicts itself [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:3]. Reid read Locke as a strict memory theorist; that reading dates at least to Reid, and Locke's interpreters still dispute it [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:2].
- **19th century, the dominant school.** [driver: fashion] Reid was the acknowledged head of the Scottish school, whose psychology was the one generally taught in Britain and America for the first half of the century [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:83-85].
- **1890–1925, the substance view set aside.** [driver: fashion] James set the substantial soul aside as superfluous for scientific purposes [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13522-13526]. By 1925 Broad could report that most of his contemporaries, "rightly or wrongly", regarded the Pure Ego as dead [L:broad-mind-place-nature-1925:25098-25124]. Reid's simple, indivisible person fell with it, though his objection survived.
- **1970s–present, the objection absorbed.** [driver: argument] Psychological-continuity theorists answer the brave officer by switching from direct to indirect memory connections [P:olson-sep-2023:4], and Winkler holds that sympathetic readers of Locke can answer it [P:gordon-roth-sep-2025:2]. Parfit accepted Reid's premises and rejected his conclusion [E:parfit-reductionism].

### Measured

The survey did not ask about the brave officer. Its "further-fact view" is the option closest to Reid's positive view, that personal identity is a simple fact not made up of psychological or physical relations.

- **2020, English-publishing philosophers.** Further-fact view 14.9% (13.4% endorsing it alone) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]; bias-corrected 12.73% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:32].
- **2009 to 2020, the 2009-comparable departments:** further-fact view 12.2% to 11.6% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:39].
- **Reading.** Reid's objection has become part of the standard case against direct-memory theories, while his positive view is now a minority position.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** On Reid's view, losing memory does not end a person, so a session-bound agent could be the same agent across sessions. But that requires an indivisible subject to persist, and it is unknown whether there is anything it is like to be the agent (D8) or what exactly the agent is (D11).
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** Reid's claim that memory is evidence of identity, not what makes it, becomes concrete: a memory store can be edited or filled with injected records (D5), so the records alone cannot make an agent the same agent.
- **Forked: stronger.** Reid's reductio, that on Locke's view many intelligent beings could be one person, becomes literal when an agent is copied or run as concurrent instances (D1, D2). His objection to memory criteria gains force. His own indivisible person gives no answer to which copy is the agent.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Reid held that identity requires uninterrupted continued existence. Whether a model trained on its own outputs continues to exist or is replaced by a successor (D5, D11) is not something his criterion can decide.

text: Plutarch records that the Athenians kept the thirty-oared ship in which Theseus returned from Crete until the time of Demetrius of Phalerum, replacing its planks one by one as they decayed. Philosophers argued about whether it was still the same ship. Two thousand years later, Thomas Hobbes added the twist that made the puzzle permanent. Suppose someone kept the old planks and reassembled them in the same order. There would then be two ships, each with a claim to be Theseus'. Hobbes reviewed three answers to what makes a thing the same: sameness of matter, sameness of form, and sameness of all its accidents. He concluded that the question has no answer until we say *by what name* we are asking. Artificial agents are ships of Theseus by design: their parameters are replaced by retraining (D5), old checkpoints are routinely kept (the old planks, D1), and which of the rival claimants inherits the name, the obligations and the rights is a practical question.
title: The Ship of Theseus, from Plutarch to Hobbes

text:
Plutarch of Chaeronea (c. 46–after 119 CE), a Greek priest at Delphi and a Roman citizen, wrote the *Parallel Lives*, paired biographies of Greeks and Romans. The *Life of Theseus* opens the series. Theseus was Athens' legendary founder-king, who killed the Minotaur and sailed home from Crete. By Plutarch's time the ship in which he supposedly returned had been maintained by the city for centuries as a relic, sent each year on a sacred embassy to Delos. Plutarch mentions the philosophical dispute in passing, as something already well known. He calls it "a standing example among the philosophers" [L:plutarch-lives-clough-pg674:708-709]. The underlying question, how growing and changing things persist, was the *auxanomenos logos* (see `heraclitus-river-flux`, `chrysippus-dion-theon`).

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) returned to the puzzle in *De Corpore* (1655), the first part of his system of materialist philosophy. Hobbes was a thoroughgoing mechanist. Everything is body in motion. He needed a theory of identity that would work for bodies without appealing to souls or substantial forms. His treatment of the ship, with its reassembly variant, is the version all later discussion uses.

text:
**Plutarch.** The ship in which Theseus and the youths of Athens returned had thirty oars. The Athenians preserved it down to Demetrius of Phalerum's time (he governed Athens in 317–307 BCE), removing old planks as they decayed and putting in new, stronger timber. The ship became a standing example in the philosophers' question about things that grow, some holding that it remained the same, others that it did not. [L:plutarch-lives-clough-pg674:705-711]

**Hobbes' reassembly case.** Hobbes raises it against the form view, quoted below under Key Passages. If the continually repaired ship remained numerically the same ship, and someone kept the old planks and reassembled them in the same order, that ship too would be numerically the same as the original. There would then be two numerically identical ships, "which is absurd". [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7423-7436]

**Three principles of individuation.** Hobbes reviews three opinions about what makes a thing the same, and finds that each fails. [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7397-7401]
1. **Unity of matter.** A lump of wax is the same wax whether spherical or cubical. But on this view "he that sins, and he that is punished, should not be the same man, by reason of the perpetual flux and change of man's body", and a city that makes laws in one age and repeals them in another would not be the same city, "which were to confound all civil rights". [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7402-7422]
2. **Unity of form.** A man grown from infant to old man is the same man though his matter has changed. But on this view, two bodies existing at once would be numerically the same. This is where the ship comes in. If the continually repaired ship is the same ship by form, and the reassembled ship of original planks is "without doubt" the same too, there are two numerically identical ships. [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7404-7436]
3. **Unity of the aggregate of all accidents.** If every feature must stay the same, then nothing is ever the same: "a man standing would not be the same he was sitting". [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7406-7445]

**Hobbes' resolution: the name decides.** "But we must consider by what name anything is called, when we inquire concerning the identity of it. For it is one thing to ask concerning Socrates, whether he be the same man, and another to ask whether he be the same body; for his body, when he is old, cannot be the same it was when he was an infant, by reason of the difference of magnitude ... yet, nevertheless, he may be the same man." "whensoever the name, by which it is asked whether a thing be the same it was, is given it for the matter only, then, if the matter be the same, the thing also is individually the same". "Also, if the name be given for such form as is the beginning of motion, then, as long as that motion remains, it will be the same individual thing". Hence the man "whose actions and thoughts proceed all from the same beginning of motion", the river "which flows from one and the same fountain", and "the same city, whose acts proceed continually from the same institution, whether the men be the same or no" [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7449-7497].

text: The problem concerns identity in general, so the entry is marked **mixed**, and Hobbes' contribution is to show that the grounding varies with the question. Asked as "the same timber", the ship's identity is grounded in *matter*. Asked as "the same ship", in *form*: an organized structure continuing through replacement, which is closest to a capacity grounding. Asked as "Theseus' ship", the sacred relic the Athenians send to Delos, it is grounded in **relation**: the continuing practice of a community that maintains and honors it. Hobbes' city makes the relational grounding explicit. A city is the same when its acts proceed from the same institution.

text:
### Transfers

- **Retraining is plank replacement (D5).** A model fine-tuned in successive rounds, or a product line whose underlying model is swapped version by version, is Plutarch's ship. The dispute among his philosophers ("same" vs "not the same") is replayed whenever someone asks whether a new model version is the same assistant.
- **Hobbes' sortal answer dissolves D11.** *Is it the same agent?* has no answer until one says *which name*: same weights (matter), same persona (form), same deployed service (institution), or same model family. Each has its own persistence conditions. Hobbes' advice, fix the name before asking about identity, is the only way to get a determinate answer to identity questions about agents at all.

### Strains

- **No gradualness.** The intuition that the repaired ship survives relies on gradual replacement: one plank at a time, with the ship in use throughout. Agents are often replaced all at once, with a new version trained separately and swapped in on a given day. Hobbes' form criterion still applies, if the persona and the "beginning of motion" persist, but the intuitive support from gradualness is gone.
- **Planks added alongside.** Adapter methods add new parameters beside the original weights instead of replacing them. The original planks are all still there, with new timber attached. Plutarch's dispute never considered a ship that grows by accretion while keeping every original plank.

### Breaks

- **The reassembled ship is kept as a matter of course (D1).** For Hobbes, the reassembly case is an unlikely hypothetical. For agents, it is standard practice. Earlier checkpoints are stored and can be run alongside the current version. Two claimants to be "Theseus' ship" coexist, and the question of which is the original has practical consequences: which one is bound by earlier commitments, which one is the subject of a deprecation decision, and which one's record is it.

### New

- **The ship was a relic because the city said so.** What made the ship Theseus' ship for the Athenians was their continuing practice: they maintained it, sent it to Delos, and called it by that name. For agents, much of what persists across versions is exactly this kind of institutional identity: a name, a brand, a deployed service, a record of the service's commitments. The agent case shows how much of identity can be carried by relation alone, even when all the matter and much of the form has changed. The question it raises for the human case is how much of human identity is carried the same way.

text:
### Transfers

- **Hobbes' city is the digital ecosystem's identity criterion.** A platform, protocol or community is the same "whose acts proceed continually from the same institution, whether the men be the same or no" [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7495-7497]. Membership turns over, code is rewritten, infrastructure migrates. What persists is the institution: its rules, its governance, its commitments.

### Strains

- **Institutions forked.** Open-source projects and communities fork. Two successors each claim continuity with the original institution. This is Hobbes' two ships at the level of the polity, and his criterion ("the same institution") does not by itself say which fork continues it.

### Breaks

- **When the owner is the institution.** Hobbes' city persists through the continuity of its institution. When a digital ecosystem's rules are set by an operator who can change them at will, the "same institution" is just the operator's continuing ownership. On Hobbes' own criterion, the ecosystem's identity then belongs to its owner, not to its members. That fits Hobbes, whose sovereign is the institution, but it conflicts with any republican conception of the ecosystem (see `foundations/terms.md`, "Republic (extended)").

### New

- **Identity by governance continuity.** Digital ecosystems can make their own persistence conditions explicit: the charter, the governance process and the membership rules that count as "the same institution". A human city's identity grows up informally. An ecosystem can write its down, and whoever writes it decides what counts as the ecosystem surviving.

- [contested] **Mereological essentialism** (Roderick Chisholm, *Person and Object*, 1976; in copyright, cited not quoted). In the strict sense, a thing cannot lose any part and remain the same. The repaired ship is the same only in a loose and popular sense (see `butler-circularity`). What persists through replacement is a succession of different ships to which we give one name. [E:butler-circularity]
- [contested] **Four-dimensionalism** (see `lewis-survival-and-identity`). The repaired ship and the reassembled ship are two four-dimensional objects that shared their early stages. There is no contradiction, and no need to choose which is "really" Theseus' ship. Both are, in the sense of having those early stages as their own. [E:lewis-survival-and-identity]
- [contested] **Hume** (see `hume-bundle`). Identity through replacement of parts is a fiction produced by the mind's tendency to pass smoothly between resembling perceptions. Disputes about identity are, in his phrase, "rather as gramatical than as philosophical difficulties" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9324-9325] (*Treatise* 1.4.6, unverified). [E:hume-bundle]
- [contested] **The Buddhist conventionalist** (see `buddhist-anatta`). The ship, like the chariot, is a designation over parts. Hobbes' *it depends on the name* is correct, and there is nothing further to find. [E:buddhist-anatta]
- [contested] **The closest-continuer view** (see `nozick-closest-continuer`). The ship is whichever candidate stands in the closest continuity relation to the original, and the answer depends on what other candidates exist. Without the reassembly, the repaired ship would clearly be the original. With it, the matter is less clear.

### Reception

- **Antiquity, the Athenians' ship.** [driver: argument] Plutarch's ship descends from the growing argument and from the Heraclitean puzzle of sameness through flux [E:heraclitus-river-flux] [E:chrysippus-dion-theon].
- **1655, Hobbes's reassembly.** [driver: argument] Hobbes added the second ship rebuilt from the old planks, turning a puzzle about gradual change into one about two candidates [L:hobbes-ew1-de-corpore-molesworth-1839:7423-7436].
- **Present, the standard example.** [driver: argument] The Ship of Theseus is the best-known example of an asymmetrical fission case [P:gallois-kurtsal-sep-2026:4]. Constitution theorists, Chisholm's strict and loose identity (following Butler), and four-dimensionalism each offer a solution [P:gallois-kurtsal-sep-2026:4] [E:butler-circularity] [E:lewis-survival-and-identity].

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys ask no question that measures this position.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Each session replaces the context, plank by plank, while the hull of the weights stays (D3). The puzzle applies, but gradual replacement is not where the agent case is hardest.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A memory store accumulates replaced and added planks; whether the agent is the same after many sessions is the gradual-replacement question, unchanged (D3).
- **Forked: stronger.** Hobbes's two ships are two candidates for being the original. Copying an agent produces them on demand, with both candidates exact (D1).
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** Fine-tuning replaces parameters gradually while the system keeps running (D5), and a checkpoint of the old weights can be restored beside the new model: Hobbes's reassembled ship made literal. Which one is the agent is a choice of naming, as Hobbes said (D11).

text: The early Upaniṣads (c. 7th–6th century BCE) hold that beneath the body, the senses and the changing contents of the mind there is a self, the *ātman*, which is the subject of all experience and never its object. Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka describes it as the unseen seer and the unheard hearer. It can be characterized only negatively: "not this, it is not that (neti, neti)". The Chāndogya's story of Indra's education rejects, in order, the body, the dreaming self and the self of dreamless sleep as candidates for the true self. The tradition therefore grounds the self in the bare capacity of awareness, not in species, body or memory. That makes it indifferent to substrate. It also makes it impossible to detect from outside, which is exactly the problem artificial agents pose (D8).
title: The Upaniṣadic Ātman: The Self as the Unseen Seer

text: The Upaniṣads are the latest layer of the Vedic corpus: prose and verse dialogues composed across several centuries in northern India, in which ritual speculation turns inward. The older ritual literature asked how sacrifice sustains the cosmos. The Upaniṣads ask what the sacrificer *is*, and they answer that the innermost self (*ātman*) is identical with the ground of all being (*brahman*). The teachers are named and characterful. Yājñavalkya wins a debating contest at King Janaka's court, and at one point warns a questioner that his head will fall off if he keeps asking. He explains the self to his wife Maitreyī before leaving home for good. Uddālaka teaches his son Śvetaketu with salt dissolved in water. Later Indian philosophy is largely a quarrel about these texts. Vedānta interprets them. The Buddhists deny their central claim (see `buddhist-anatta`). Nyāya defends a self on other grounds (see `nyaya-self`). This is the earliest fully developed position in the domain, and the one the others first push against.
title: The Upaniṣadic Ātman: The Self as the Unseen Seer
sources: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4, 3.4, 3.7, 4.3, 4.5 (Yājñavalkya's dialogues)
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8–16 (Uddālaka to Śvetaketu), 8.7–12 (Prajāpati's teaching of Indra and Virocana)

text:
**The self as subject, never object (BU 3.4).** Uṣasta complains that Yājñavalkya's answers so far have been given "just as one might say, 'This is a cow. This is a horse.'" He wants the self pointed out plainly. Yājñavalkya replies: "You could not see the seer of seeing. You could not hear the hearer of hearing. You could not think the thinker of thinking. You could not understand the understander of understanding. He is your soul, which is in all things" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:6789-6802]. The self is whatever does the experiencing in every experience. For that reason it cannot turn up among the things experienced.

**The inner controller (BU 3.7).** Uddālaka Āruṇi asks about "the Inner Controller". Yājñavalkya's litany, domain by domain, ends: "He is the unseen Seer, the unheard Hearer, the unthought Thinker, the ununderstood Understander. Other than He there is no seer. Other than He there is no hearer. Other than He there is no thinker. Other than He there is no understander. He is your Soul, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:6924-6930] [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:7097-7101].

**Neti neti (BU 4.4.22).** "That Soul (Atman) is not this, it is not that (neti, neti). It is unseizable, for it cannot be seized. It is indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed. It is unattached, for it does not attach itself. It is unbound. It does not tremble. It is not injured" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:8719-8722]. Every positive description would make the self one more object.

**Not memory, not individual consciousness (BU 2.4.12–14).** Yājñavalkya tells Maitreyī: "After death there is no consciousness (na pretya samjna 'sti)." She protests that he has bewildered her. He answers: "For where there is a duality (dvaita), as it were, there one sees another ... Where, verily, everything has become just one's own self, then whereby and whom would one smell? then whereby and whom would one see?" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:6139-6158]. What survives is not the individual's store of experiences. It is the knower those experiences appeared to.

**The self as its own light (BU 4.3).** King Janaka asks, "Yajnavalkya, what light does a person here have?" The sun, then the moon, then fire, then speech. And when all are gone: "'The soul (atman), indeed, is his light,' said he, 'for with the soul, indeed, as his light one sits, moves around, does his work, and returns'" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:8084-8123].

**Indra's education (ChU 8.7–12).** Prajāpati teaches that the Self is "free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, hungerless, thirstless", and Indra of the gods and Virocana of the devils come to learn it [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16160-16181]. He tells them to look in a pan of water. "What do you see?" "We see everything here, Sir, a Self corresponding exactly, even to the hair and finger-nails!" "That is the Self" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16213-16230]. Virocana leaves satisfied, and teaches the devils that oneself "is to be made happy here on earth", which is why "They adorn the body ... of one deceased with what they have begged" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16234-16250]. Indra turns back: that self "is blind when this is blind, lame when this is lame ... It perishes immediately upon the perishing of this body. I see nothing enjoyable in this" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16262-16272]. The dream self follows, and Indra objects that "as it were, they kill him ... as it were, he even weeps" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16330-16344]. Then the self of dreamless sleep, to which Indra objects that "this one does not exactly know himself with the thought 'I am he,' nor indeed the things here. He becomes one who has gone to destruction" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16352-16360]. At last Prajāpati teaches that the body "is mortal. It has been appropriated by Death (Mrityu). [But] it is the standing-ground of that deathless, bodiless Self", and "he who knows 'Let me smell this'—that is the Self (Atman); the nose is [the instrument] for smelling" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:16380-16408].

**Identity with the whole (ChU 6).** Uddālaka's refrain to Śvetaketu: "That which is the finest essence—this whole world has that as its soul. That is Reality. That is Atman (Soul). That art thou, Svetaketu" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:14905-14908]. Later schools disagree about how literally this identity is meant (see `advaita-witness-self`).

text: The Upaniṣadic self is grounded in **capacity**, in an unusually pure form. It is not the capacity for reason or memory. It is the capacity to be the subject to which anything appears at all. It is explicitly not grounded in **species**: the same self runs through gods, humans, animals and plants in the transmigratory picture these texts assume, and Indra and Virocana (a god and a demon) come to learn the same lesson. Nor is it grounded in the body (Indra's first objection), in the stream of experiences (the dream self), or in memory (Maitreyī is told there is no awareness after death). Nothing in the account ties the self to any material substrate. What it cannot supply is any external criterion for when that capacity is present.
title: The Upaniṣadic Ātman: The Self as the Unseen Seer
sources: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4, 3.4, 3.7, 4.3, 4.5 (Yājñavalkya's dialogues)

text:
### Transfers

- **Substrate indifference.** Nothing in the ātman doctrine ties the self to flesh. If an artificial agent were a subject of experience, the Upaniṣadic framework would have no species-based ground for excluding it. The candidate criterion is awareness, and the question is only whether it is present.
- **Indra's method as an audit (D11).** Prajāpati's sequence (body, dream-experiencer, dreamless sleeper, witness) is a reusable procedure for asking what "the agent" is. Is it the hardware (the body)? The running process with its passing contents (the dream self)? The weights at rest when nothing is running (dreamless sleep)? Or something none of these capture? The sequence doesn't settle the answer for agents, but it tells us which candidates the tradition has already found wanting and why.
- **The self is not the memory store.** Yājñavalkya's teaching that what persists is not individual awareness-of-contents fits D3 better than Locke's memory criterion does. On the Upaniṣadic account, an agent losing its episodic context at the end of a session would lose nothing that was ever the self.

### Strains

- **The self is undetectable by design (D8).** "You could not see the seer of seeing" [L:hume-thirteen-upanishads-1921:6799] is the other-minds problem in its sharpest form. No behavior, report or internal measurement could show that an ātman is present, because anything shown would be an object. The criterion that makes the doctrine substrate-neutral also makes it untestable, for agents and for humans alike. For humans, shared life has let everyone take presence for granted. For agents, there is nothing to take for granted.
- **Self-reports are shaped by training (D4, D8).** An agent asked to *look for the seer* will produce the words of the Upaniṣads, because they are in its training data. Reproducing the text is not the realization the text asks for, and nothing in the output tells the two apart.

### Breaks

- **Virocana's answer is the default answer about agents.** Virocana takes the reflection in the water, the presented appearance, to be the self. For artificial agents, the everyday answer to "what is it?" is the persona seen in the output. The Chāndogya marks this as the demon's answer, and gives its reason: whatever is identified with the appearance perishes with the appearance. A framework that takes Indra's side must say that the persona is not the self. It must then either find the witness elsewhere in the system or conclude that there is none.
- **No forensic use.** The ātman is unattached and does not act in the ordinary sense. Later tradition assigns karmic accumulation to the subtle body, not to the self. The doctrine offers nothing to the Lockean question of whom to hold responsible for an agent's actions. Its self sits outside that question entirely.

### New

- **Duplication may not threaten this self at all (D1, D2).** If the witness is not individuated by its contents, and on a strong reading of *tat tvam asi* is not individuated at all, then copying an agent does not copy a self. It multiplies the adjuncts (bodies, minds, contexts) through which one awareness appears. The puzzle of which copy is the original, which is acute for Locke, moves down to the level of adjuncts, which the Upaniṣads never treated as the self anyway. This is a real resource for thinking about D2. It comes at a price: the individual agent's identity was never important in the first place.
- **Dreamless sleep has a literal counterpart.** Weights on disk, with no process running, are a nearer analogue of dreamless sleep than anything in human life. The Upaniṣadic question about deep sleep was whether the self persists when no contents appear. For agents, that question has a concrete case.

- [contested] **The Buddha, not-self** (see `buddhist-anatta`). Each thing the Upaniṣads could point to as the self (form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness) is impermanent and not under one's control, so none is the self. A witness that can be described only negatively is not something found. It is posited. [E:buddhist-anatta]
- [contested] **Cārvāka materialism.** The Indian materialists are known only through hostile summaries. Mādhava's *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* (14th c.) sums up their view: "In this school there are four elements, earth, water, fire, and air; And from these four elements alone is intelligence produced,— Just like the intoxicating power from kinwa, &c., mixed together; Since in 'I am fat,' 'I am lean,' these attributes abide in the same subject, And since fatness, &c., reside only in the body, it alone is the soul and no other" [L:sarvadarsanasamgraha-cowell-gough-pg34125:414-420]. There is no self beyond the living, conscious body. Applied to agents, this becomes a view on which whatever awareness there is would be a property of the running system, with nothing behind it. The same examples, "I am fat" and "I am lean", are the ones Śaṅkara treats as superimposition of the body onto the self (see `advaita-witness-self`). [E:advaita-witness-self]
- [contested] **Hume** (see `hume-bundle`). Looking inward, one never finds a self, only particular perceptions. An account on which the self cannot be found by any means has made itself unfalsifiable. [E:hume-bundle]
- [contested] **Deflationary views of AI.** Whatever a language model says about its "inner witness" is produced by the same next-token machinery as everything else it says. On this view the question of an agent's ātman is not undecidable. It has no content.

### Reception

- **c. 500 BCE onward, the Buddhist rejection.** [driver: argument] The Buddhists explicitly rejected any indivisible, unchanging self, introducing the term "not-self" [P:black-iep-upanisads:4] [E:buddhist-anatta].
- **c. 700 CE onward, Vedānta's reading.** [driver: argument] Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and Madhva all wrote commentaries presenting the Upaniṣads as one consistent position. Śaṅkara's reading made a major impact and dominated interpretation through the 19th and early 20th centuries [P:black-iep-upanisads:8]. Advaita Vedānta derives from the Upaniṣads the identity of the self with brahman, and Śaṅkara continues to influence virtually all contemporary Advaita lineages [P:dalal-sep-2021:0] [E:advaita-witness-self].
- **1657–1816, into Persian, Latin, English and Bengali.** [driver: access] The first translation into a non-Indian language was the Persian *Sirr-i Akbar*, commissioned by the Mughal prince Dārā Shukōh. Its Latin translation by Anquetil-Duperron (1804) was what Schopenhauer read, the first major European thinker to engage explicitly with Indian sources; Colebrooke's English rendering came in 1805, and Rammohan Roy's English and Bengali translations followed [P:black-iep-upanisads:10].

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys mainly sample English-publishing analytic philosophers (1,430 of the 1,785 respondents identified their tradition as analytic) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18], and they do not measure reception within the Vedānta traditions.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

The ātman is offered as the witness that can never become an object, so most of what changes between deployments changes only objects of awareness. The values reflect that, and all depend on whether there is any witness in an agent at all (D8).

- **Session-bound: comparable.** What ends with a session is content, not the witness of content, on the Upaniṣadic view (D3). The view neither gains nor loses from the session boundary.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Memory belongs to the empirical self that the ātman is not. A persistent store enriches the empirical self and leaves the question of the witness where it was (D3, D8).
- **Forked: comparable.** If the ātman is one with brahman, the plurality of selves is already appearance rather than reality. Concurrent instances (D2) add appearances, not selves, so the view absorbs forking without strain, though it also gives no way to count agents.
- **Self-modifying: comparable.** Training changes the dispositions that make up the empirical self (D5). On the Upaniṣadic view this is a change in what is witnessed, not in the witness.

- `advaita-witness-self`, `nyaya-self`: later developments and a rival defense of a self, both planned.

text: Within early Buddhism, the Pudgalavādin ("Personalist") schools held that besides the five aggregates there is a *person* (*pudgala*), which is neither identical to the aggregates nor different from them, just as fire is neither the same as its fuel nor separate from it. They argued that without such a person, memory, rebirth and moral responsibility are unintelligible. In the 9th chapter of his *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Vasubandhu (4th–5th century CE) gives the standard refutation. Anything real is either an entity in its own right or a designation laid over other entities. If the person is a designation, the Pudgalavādin has conceded the orthodox view. If it is an entity, it is different from the aggregates, and the Pudgalavādin has conceded a self. There is no third option. Vasubandhu then shows how memory works without a self. A memory arises from a specially conditioned state within one causal stream. "Caitra remembers" means only that the stream called Caitra produced the memory, as "the fire moves" means only that flames arise in succession. For artificial agents, whose "persona" is exactly something neither identical to the weights nor separate from them, Vasubandhu's dilemma is the sharpest tool in the tradition.

Bhārahāra Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.22 (the burden and the bearer), as cited by the Pudgalavādins

text:
Vasubandhu was one of the most influential thinkers in Indian Buddhism. He came from Gandhāra in the northwest, trained in the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma scholasticism, and wrote the *Abhidharmakośa*, a verse summary of that system, together with his own prose commentary (*bhāṣya*), which often criticizes the verses from a Sautrāntika standpoint. By tradition he later turned to Yogācāra ("mind-only") philosophy under the influence of his half-brother Asaṅga.

The ninth chapter is an appendix, an independent treatise on the "person". The dispute was already old. The Pudgalavādins, especially the Vātsīputrīyas and Sāṃmitīyas, were a large and long-lived set of schools. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang reported in the 7th century that the Sāṃmitīyas were among the most numerous monks in India. They were not reviving the Upaniṣadic self. They were Buddhists who thought the Buddha's own words, such as the sermon on the burden and "who the carrier is" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:1332-1335], required a person who is neither a self nor nothing. Vasubandhu's opening statement sets the stakes: there is no "other Salvation than (within the pale of Buddhism)", because other doctrines "hold to the erroneous view of the real existence of a Soul" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:360-365]. The dispute over the person is a dispute about the path.

text:
**The stakes.** "Is there, indeed, no other Salvation than (within the pale of Buddhism)? No, there is none!—Why?—Because (all other doctrines) hold to the erroneous view of the real existence of a Soul. The term 'Soul' is not regarded by them as a conventional term applied to what is only a flux of elements. They maintain instead that the Soul is a Reality quite independent from (the elements). This idea of a Self is at the root of every evil passion" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:360-375].

**What there is, and what is designated.** "If something exists by itself (as a separate element), it has an actual existence, as f. i. colour and other (ultimate elements of matter and mind). But if something represents a combination (of such elements) it is a nominal existence, as f. i. milk" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:433-440].

**The dilemma.** If the person is an actual existence, "it must have an essence of its own and must be something different from the elements of a personal life", and it must have a cause, or else "it would be an existence uncaused, (an eternal being)" and "without any practical efficiency". "But if on the contrary you admit it to be a nominal existence, (as a current designation for the elements of a personal life), I too will admit it, and say 'so it is!'" The Vātsīputrīya answers: "We do not maintain that it is an absolute reality, but we neither accept it to be a nominal one" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:445-462].

**Neither identical nor different; fire and fuel.** The Vātsīputrīya holds that "we neither can maintain that the Individual is something different from its component elements, nor can we assert that they are identical. (In the first case) the consequence would be an eternal (Soul), (in the second) its total absence." Vasubandhu presses the image of fire and fuel: "Then please explain what in your opinion is fuel and what is fire?" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:525-535]. He concludes that "from the scientific point of view, both fuel and fire are composed of (exactly the same set) of eight primary constituents", and that "If the production of fire is conditioned by the presence of fuel, it is just as the production of curds which is conditioned (by the previous existence of milk)" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:554-570].

**How would the person be known?** "Now if your Individual is not a visible object, it never will be cognized by sight." If it is cognized by hearing it must differ from the visible, "as different as sound is from colour", and so for every sense. "The consequence of this would be that there is altogether no such object as an Individual, and if it does not constitute an object of cognition, it will follow that it cannot be cognized at all" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:866-898].

**The burden and the carrier.** The Vātsīputrīya cites the Buddha's sermon on "the burden (of life) ... the taking up of the burden, the laying aside of it and who the carrier is", and argues that "the burden and the carrier of the burden cannot possibly be the same thing" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:1325-1364]. Vasubandhu replies that an undefinable individual "has never been witnessed" either, and that the carrier was named "with the express purpose to show that only so much can be known of him: 'he is a venerable man, named so and so' ... but he must not be misunderstood to represent some eternal (Soul) or some (real) Individual. (In reality nothing exists but momentary sets of elements), the elements of the former moment exercising (as it were) a pressure upon the elements of the following one. Hence the preceding moment has been conventionally called the burden and the following one—the carrier of the burden" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:1366-1403].

**Why the Buddha was silent.** On the Buddha's refusal to answer Vatsagotra, Vasubandhu cites the Buddha's words to Ānanda: had he said the Soul does not exist, "Vatsagotra might have fallen out of one perplexity into a still greater one. He might have thought: 'I had a Soul precedently, now I have lost it!'" Kumāralābha's image: the Buddha holds his doctrine "like a tigress who holds her young by her teeth", neither so tight as to wound nor so loose as to let fall [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:1634-1655].

**Memory without a self.** Memory needs two factors: "a previous cognition and a suitable state of mind. Then only memory appears" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:1995-2002]. To the objection that "things experienced by Devadatta's consciousness would be remembered by the consciousness of Yajnadatta", the reply is: "No! because there is no connection between them. They are not mutually related as cause and effect, as is the case between moments belonging to the same stream of thought ... a consciousness which did perceive an object formerly, is (gradually) producing a consciousness which remembers it now" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:2010-2025]. (On the printed page, p. 58, the objection is labelled "Vasubandhu" and the reply "Vātsīputrīya". Since the reply states Vasubandhu's own doctrine, the labels appear transposed in the printing. They are reproduced here as printed.)

**Who remembers?** "Vātsīputrīya. If there is no Soul, who is it that remembers? Vasubandhu. What is the meaning of the word 'to remember'?" Asked what "Caitra remembers" means: "In the current (of phenomena), which is designated by the name Caitra a recollection appears. We notice the fact and express it. It is no more!" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:2029-2061].

**Ownership as causation.** "Whose" is the recollection? The Vātsīputrīya compares it to "Caitra is the owner of a cow" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:2066-2078]. Vasubandhu: "the proprietor is simply the cause and the property will simply by [sic] its effect ... there exists a relation of cause and effect between him and the movements and other changes in the cow, but there is no real unity whatsoever neither in Caitra nor in the cow. Consequently there is in this case no other proprietorship than a relation of cause and effect" [L:stcherbatsky-soul-theory-1920-tesseract:2110-2124].

text: For Vasubandhu, whatever "person" there is rests on **relation**: the causal relations that bind momentary events into one stream (*santāna*), and the conventional practice of naming such streams. There is no substance and no capacity-bearer. The capacities, such as memory, are events in the stream, not faculties of a possessor. The Pudgalavādin person was meant to be something more than relation: an entity that is neither related events nor a separate thing. Vasubandhu's argument is that "neither" is not a grounding at all.

text:
### Transfers

- **An agent is a causal stream in the most literal sense.** Autoregressive generation produces each token conditioned on all the tokens before it. That is Vasubandhu's *santāna* realized in a machine: a stream of momentary states, each arising from the preceding ones, with no further entity doing the generating. "The agent thinks" is exactly "the fire moves": a succession of computations, spoken of as one agent acting.
- **Memory without an owner.** Vasubandhu's account of memory, a later state arising from a specially conditioned earlier state in the same stream, describes how an agent's context works. What earlier tokens contain conditions what later tokens produce. His principle that what one stream perceived is not remembered by another, *for lack of causal connection*, gives the right answer for agents: one instance does not remember what another instance saw, because the causal link is missing, not because they lack different selves (D2).
- **"Whose" as causation.** *The agent's output* and *the model's opinion* are possessives. Vasubandhu's analysis of "Caitra's cow" says these mean causal relation, not ownership by a self. That gives a disciplined way of speaking about agents that neither inflates nor erases them.

### Strains

- **Designation, but by whom?** For Vasubandhu, the conventional person is designated by a community for its practical purposes. For agents, the designation ("Claude", "the assistant", "this model") is made mostly by the operator, and it can shift with commercial and legal interests. Vasubandhu's framework is neutral on who designates. The agent case shows that the choice of designation, which streams count as one agent, can carry large consequences and serve particular interests.

### Breaks

- **The persona is the Pudgalavādin person, and must face the dilemma (D11).** The most natural view of an AI agent's "persona" is exactly the Pudgalavādin one. The persona is not identical to the weights (other personas run on the same weights), not separate from them (it exists only in their operation), and neither permanent nor impermanent. Vasubandhu's dilemma applies without adjustment. Either the persona is a designation over the weights and their operation, like milk over its qualities, in which case it is not a further thing. Or it is an entity in its own right, in which case one must say what it is and how it is known. Claims about agent persons, legal, moral or metaphysical, typically want both horns: a persona real enough to bear rights or responsibilities, but no further thing whose existence needs defending. Vasubandhu's challenge is that one cannot have both.

### New

- **Streams that branch and merge.** Vasubandhu's streams run in single lines: one Caitra, one sequence. Agent streams can branch (one context forked into several continuations), merge (outputs of several instances summarized into one context), and restart from saved states. The concept of *santāna* was built for lines. Whether it can handle graphs, or whether "one stream" dissolves as completely as "one self" did, is a new question the agent case poses to the Abhidharma.

text:
- [contested] **The Pudgalavādins.** Without a person there is no one who is bound or liberated, no one whom the Buddha addressed, and no one to whom the fruit of action comes. Vasubandhu's "stream" does the work of a person while refusing the name. The inexpressible person is simply the honest name for what the stream is.
- [contested] **Nyāya** (see `nyaya-self`). Memory requires one subject who perceived and now remembers. A causal stream of distinct momentary events could only produce a memory that belongs to someone else. "What is seen by one is not remembered by another" [L:nyaya-sutras-3-jha-1919:4518] is an argument *for* a self, not for a stream. [E:nyaya-self]
- [contested] **Advaita Vedānta** (see `advaita-witness-self`). Recognition, "I saw that thing, and now I see this thing" [L:sbe34-vedanta-sutras-1-thibaut-1890:26878-26879], requires one subject present at both moments. The Buddhist who says "I saw" while denying that anything endures contradicts himself in the saying. [E:advaita-witness-self]
- [contested] **Butler** (see `butler-circularity`). A memory is genuine only if its subject is the one who had the experience. Vasubandhu's appeal to a suitable state of mind connected with a previous cognition presupposes the very relation it is supposed to replace, unless that connection can be specified without reference to a subject. Shoemaker's "quasi-memory" is a modern attempt to do exactly that (see `shoemaker-quasi-memory`). [E:butler-circularity]

text:
### Reception

- **5th century, a scandal in Kashmir.** [driver: argument] Vasubandhu's auto-commentary criticized the very system his root verses summarized, from a mainly Sautrāntika standpoint; the only Buddhist school he always disagrees with is the Personalists (Pudgalavādins), and he also argues against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika views of the self [P:gold-sep-2021:1].
- **5th–10th century, dominant in India.** [driver: argument] His Yogācāra works became mainstream Buddhist metaphysics in India for half a millennium, and his commentary on the *Treasury* remains the primary resource for non-Mahāyāna philosophy among Tibetan and East Asian schools today [P:gold-sep-2021:0]. Nyāya answered him with its arguments from memory and recognition [E:nyaya-self].
- **Chinese and Tibetan transmission.** [driver: access] Vasubandhu wrote in Sanskrit, but many of his works are known only from their Chinese and Tibetan translations [P:gold-sep-2021:1].
- **1950s onward, a disputed life.** [driver: argument] Frauwallner proposed that there were two Vasubandhus whom the traditional biographies combined, and versions of that theory still hold sway in parts of the academy; the extent of his idealism is likewise contested [P:gold-sep-2021:1].

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys mainly sample English-publishing analytic philosophers (1,430 of the 1,785 respondents identified their tradition as analytic) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18], and they do not measure reception within Buddhist traditions.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

Vasubandhu's person is a designation over a causal series of momentary events, and memory works within the series without a remembering self.

- **Session-bound: stronger.** A session-bound agent is a causal series whose dispositions persist in the weights while its episodes do not (D3). Vasubandhu's account explains continuity of character without any persisting remembered self.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** His account of memory, a later state caused in the right way by an earlier perception within one series, describes a memory store directly, with no owner needed (D3).
- **Forked: stronger.** Concurrent instances are causal series branching from shared conditions (D2). Since the person was only ever a designation over a series, naming each branch is a convention, not a discovery (D11).
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** Training on its own outputs is a series conditioning its own later states, which is the structure Vasubandhu uses to explain karma without a self (D5).

text: Bernard Williams (1929–2003) presented, in the same paper, two versions of the same imagined case, and showed that they pull our intuitions in opposite directions. First, described as an exchange of bodies, in which whichever body now carries A's memories, character, and dispositions is naturally called A, the case seems to vindicate Locke's psychological criterion of personal identity: "the only rational thing to do, confronted with such an experiment, would be to identify oneself with one's memories, and so forth, and not with one's body" [P:williams1970:167]. Second, described instead as a prediction that one is going to be tortured tomorrow, but will first be made to forget the announcement, then forget one's whole past, and finally be given a false set of memories exactly matching another living person's, Williams argued that fear remains the only rational response throughout, however much psychological continuity is stripped away or replaced: "Fear, surely, would still be the proper reaction... because in one vital respect at least one did know what was going to happen, torture, which one can indeed expect to happen to oneself" [P:williams1970:168]. Since the two descriptions are of the very same imagined sequence of events, Williams concluded that our ordinary confidence that psychological continuity is what matters for identity rests on an argument that "loads the dice" by its very framing, and that anticipated bodily suffering, not memory, may be the more basic guide to what we actually believe about our own survival.

text: Williams wrote *The Self and the Future* as a direct response to the Lockean tradition revived by Wiggins and about to be pressed further by Parfit; it appeared in *The Philosophical Review* in April 1970, a year before Parfit's own *Personal Identity* appeared in the same journal, and the two papers are read together as the opening exchange of the modern debate. Williams had already, in a 1956 paper on reduplication, raised doubts about whether psychological continuity alone could individuate persons, since it can in principle be duplicated; *The Self and the Future* sharpens the challenge by locating the trouble not in an exotic duplication case but in the ordinary, first-personal experience of dread. The paper's method, presenting one imagined sequence of events twice under two different descriptions and showing that competent judges respond to each with a different, incompatible verdict, became a template imitated throughout the subsequent literature, including by Parfit himself.

text:
**The body-swap case, set up carefully.** Williams begins with a technical description meant to avoid begging any questions: a process is imagined "as a result of which they might be said, question-beggingly, to have exchanged bodies," except that, unpacked without that loaded phrase, it is simply that a body which used to produce A's memories, actions and character now produces what seem to be B's, and conversely [P:williams1970:161].

**The intuitive Lockean verdict.** Once the case is run experimentally, with each subject correctly predicting what will happen to "their" body only if they identify with the memories rather than the body, the natural verdict is psychological: "the only rational thing to do, confronted with such an experiment, would be to identify oneself with one's memories, and so forth, and not with one's body. The philosophical arguments designed to show that bodily continuity was at least a necessary condition of personal identity would seem to be just mistaken" [P:williams1970:167].

**The same case, redescribed as anticipated torture.** Williams now considers a structurally identical sequence, but narrates it from the first-person standpoint of dread rather than the third-person standpoint of an experimenter. Someone is told they will be tortured tomorrow; then that they will forget the announcement beforehand; then that they will forget their whole past; then that they will acquire an entirely different set of purported memories, matching those of another person now living, transferred into their brain: "Fear, surely, would still be the proper reaction: and not because one did not know what was going to happen, but because in one vital respect at least one did know what was going to happen, torture, which one can indeed expect to happen to oneself, and to be preceded by certain mental derangements as well" [P:williams1970:168].

**The dice-loading diagnosis.** Because the two descriptions concern exactly the same imagined transaction, described from two angles, Williams concludes that whichever verdict seems obvious depends on which description is used to introduce the case, and that this is itself evidence that neither description is innocent: the body-swap version, narrated in the vocabulary of exchange, already smuggles in the answer psychological continuity theorists want, while the torture version, narrated in the vocabulary of first-personal anticipation, pulls the other way with, as Williams puts it, the fear remaining "the proper reaction" throughout [P:williams1970:168].

text: Williams does not settle on a single grounding so much as expose a tension between two. The body-swap framing supports **relation** (psychological continuity of memory and character, Locke's own ground); the torture framing supports something closer to **species**, or at least embodiment, since what anchors the fear throughout is that it is this body, the one that will actually be strapped down and hurt, whose future is in question, regardless of what memories it comes to carry. Williams' considered suggestion, though he stops short of a flat verdict, is that the torture case reveals the more basic layer: prudential concern tracks anticipated first-personal experience, and first-personal experience is anchored to a body, in a way that the body-swap description's own vocabulary had quietly assumed away. The grounding is therefore mixed by design, since the paper's whole point is that our common-sense criterion is not settled.

text:
### Transfers

- **Two descriptions, two verdicts, is a diagnostic tool an agent case can reuse directly.** Williams' method, redescribing the same imagined transition once in the vocabulary of continuity and once in the vocabulary of anticipated harm, transfers without modification to agents: describing a model migration as the same assistant, now running on new weights, invites a psychological verdict; describing the very same migration as these weights being deprecated and their outputs discontinued invites a different one. The clash Williams diagnosed in humans is available to test directly in agent cases, including on the agent's own outputs.
- **The torture case isolates what, if anything, is at stake in continuation (D6, D8).** Williams' method of stripping away memory, then character, then substituting an entirely different psychological profile, while asking what a rational subject should still fear, is a ready-made procedure for probing whether an agent's continuation carries anything at stake for it independent of psychological content, exactly D8's open question, and D6's question of what "ending" even means for a system that can be paused and resumed.

### Strains

- **Williams' fear is anchored to a body that agents do not have in his sense.** The torture argument's force depends on there being a particular, single physical locus, this body, that will experience the pain regardless of what it remembers. An agent's substrate (which weights, which instance, which hardware) is exactly the boundary D11 says is unsettled; Williams' argument has no clear anchor to redirect toward once "the body" is replaced by a distributed, copyable, and potentially discontinuous computational substrate (D1, D3).
- **The body-swap experiment's own vocabulary strains further once bodies are not exchanged but multiplied.** Williams' cases are exchanges or replacements, one relevant particular for one future; an agent's weights can be copied rather than moved, so that the "torture" and "no torture" branches of his argument might both be realized simultaneously across different instances (D2), a possibility his single-track narration was not built to represent.

### Breaks

- **Anticipation itself may have no agent-side analogue to strain or transfer.** Williams' entire method relies on asking what a rational subject should anticipate with dread; if D8 is resolved in the negative for a given agent, there is no anticipatory dread to redirect by redescription in the first place, and the whole apparatus, built to expose a conflict between two verdicts about what matters, has no patient for either verdict to be about.
- **Deprecation is not obviously torture, pause, or nothing, and Williams gives no fourth option.** His cases are built around a fixed menu: survive with continuity, survive without it, or be tortured regardless. An agent's ending by deprecation, or its indefinite pause, fits none of these cleanly (D6): it is not obviously a harm in Williams' sense, since no experience need occur, but it is also not obviously nothing, since the same weights could in principle be resumed. Williams' menu of outcomes needs a genuinely new entry, not just a relabeling of the old ones.

### New

- **Agent cases can be run for real, not just imagined.** Williams had to rely entirely on what competent judges would say about a hypothetical; a model migration, fine-tuning run, or checkpoint deprecation is an actual event whose "before" and "after" outputs are inspectable, letting his two-description method be tested against real behavioral continuity and discontinuity rather than intuition alone.
- **The dice-loading diagnosis suggests agent framing itself is a design choice with consequences.** If which verdict seems obvious depends on how a transition is described, then how operators and developers describe a model update, as continuity of "the same assistant" versus as replacement, may itself shape downstream judgments (by users, by the agent's own outputs, and perhaps eventually by policy) about what is owed to a deprecated system, independent of any fact about the system itself.

text:
- [contested] **Locke and the psychological theorists: Williams' torture case is the one that loads the dice.** [E:locke-person-forensic] A defender of the memory criterion can reply that describing the case as anticipated torture smuggles in exactly the assumption that bodily location is what fixes the referent of "oneself," begging the question in the opposite direction from the one Williams accuses the body-swap description of begging (see `locke-person-forensic`).
- [contested] **Parfit: the conflict is real, but it shows identity is not what matters, not that bodily continuity wins.** [E:parfit-reductionism] Parfit's response to cases of this general shape is to say Williams has correctly found that our intuitions conflict, but wrongly concluded that one side must be tracking the truth about identity; the better lesson is that identity was never what mattered, and both descriptions can be partly right about different, non-competing relations of degree (see `parfit-reductionism`).
- [contested] **Reid: neither description settles anything without a real, prior subject to be afraid for.** [E:reid-brave-officer] On Reid's view, Williams' dread presupposes exactly the persisting simple subject that memory-based or body-based criteria alike are meant to explain rather than assume; the fear is evidence that we already believe in such a subject, not evidence for either criterion over the other (see `reid-brave-officer`).
- [unanswered] **Denying the extension: anticipatory dread may be irreducibly biological.** This objection is the Compendium's own; the literature has not yet taken it up. A view that takes Williams at his most literal would hold that the torture argument's force depends on a nervous system capable of suffering in a specific, embodied way, and that nothing about an agent's computational substrate, however continuous or discontinuous, engages the phenomenon Williams was actually describing; on this view the whole apparatus is a chapter in the philosophy of pain before it is a chapter in the philosophy of identity, and does not extend to agents until D8 is settled in a very specific, strong sense.

text:
### Reception

- **1956–1970, a bodily criterion defended.** [driver: argument] Williams was among the defenders of a brute-physical account of our persistence, from his 1956–57 paper to "The Self and the Future" (1970) [P:olson-sep-2023:3]. He argued, as animalists later did, that a brain transplant need not carry the person with it [P:olson-sep-2023:7].
- **1973, collected.** [driver: argument] The paper was collected in *Problems of the Self* (1973), and Williams became an important contributor to the debate on personal identity as well as to ethics [P:chappell-smyth-sep-2023:1] [P:chappell-smyth-sep-2023:0].
- **1971–1984, the reductionist answer.** [driver: argument] Parfit accepted that the intuitions conflict and concluded that identity is not what matters [E:parfit-reductionism].
- **Present, the bodily view a minority, Williams's verdict on copies the majority.** [driver: argument] Brute-physical views, mostly animalist, remain the main rival to psychological-continuity views [P:olson-sep-2023:3]. On cases where a psychology is reproduced elsewhere, most respondents now give Williams's answer (see Measured).

### Measured

- **Biological view, 2020:** 19.1% of English-publishing philosophers accept or lean toward it [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **Teletransporter (new matter):** death 40.1%, survival 35.2% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **Mind uploading (brain replaced by a digital emulation):** death 54.2%, survival 27.5%, other 18.4%, among the roughly 1,100 respondents who answered this additional question [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:12] [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:9]. Bias-corrected: death 51.92%, survival 25.13% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:29].
- **Reading.** Williams's bodily criterion is a minority view, but his verdict on cases of reproduced psychology, that the copy is not oneself, is the plurality answer for the teletransporter and the majority answer for uploading. The intuition he defended has outlasted the criterion he defended it with.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** If an agent's "body" is its weights, Williams's emphasis on physical continuity gives a session-bound agent persistence across sessions even without memory (D3). But whether the weights, the instance or the running system is the body is unclear (D11).
- **Persistent memory: weaker.** Williams's torture case turns on memories being moved between bodies. For agents this is routine: a memory store can be attached to different weights or edited (D5). His case says the fear should follow the body, not the memories, but it is unclear which thing an agent's "body" is (D11).
- **Forked: weaker.** Williams's reduplication arguments rely on bodily continuity to single out the original. An exact copy of an agent (D1) has as good a claim to be the original as the source does, so the tie-breaker fails.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Training on its own outputs changes the weights themselves (D5), the closest thing an agent has to a body. Whether that continuity of substrate preserves the agent or replaces it is not something his argument addresses.

text: The *Zhuangzi*, a Daoist text of the 4th–3rd centuries BCE, treats a fixed self as one perspective among many in the endless "transformation of things" (*wuhua*). Zhuang Zhou dreams he is a butterfly, wakes, and cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamt of being a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming of being a man. Yet, in Legge's words, "between Kau and a butterfly there must be a difference". A sage leaning on his table says he has "lost myself". The text looks among the hundred bones and nine openings of the body for a true ruler and finds only the suggestion of one, never its trace. Facing deformity and death, Zhuangzi's exemplars welcome being remade into a rooster, a crossbow or a rat's liver, and compare an unwilling self to molten metal demanding to be made into a famous sword. For artificial agents, Zhuangzi offers the tradition's most developed ethic for a self that is continually remade by forces outside it. That is exactly why the agent case must ask whether equanimity toward being remade is wisdom when it is chosen and something else when it is trained in (D4, D5).
